### W111 · NUC sustained durable-write slowdown: filesystem, device and queue attribution

**Class/state:** performance investigation; open. **Assigned cluster:** NUC.
Split from W97 by user request on Oct 11, 2026. This is not an AMD admission
acceptance gate. The bounded AMD unpaced overload/admission work is closed;
W97's independent replication-feedback acceptance remains separate.

**Finding:** Durable tiny-file throughput falls over sustained NUC runs while
server sync and device completion latency rise. EFS-stopped controls also show
a NVMe decline on fully written extents, so allocation alone does not explain
it. XFS journal work, block scheduling/queueing and device/cache behaviour
still need discrimination. No hardware ceiling or cache/firmware cause has
been established, and stable raw SATA controls do not repair the earlier EFS
SATA slowdown.

**Evidence transferred from W97 (historical observations unchanged):**

**Oct11 NUC isolated follow-up:** two eight-minute growing-file repeats outside
EFS reproduce aggregate430/428→188/186 durable64KiB writes/s, per-writer mean
sync~6.9→~16ms. Preallocated-ring repeats finish near438ops/s, with materially
different initial windows and tails. Allocation/overwrite behaviour matters,
but XFS versus drive/cache attribution is not yet isolated. All eight allocation cells, four separate XFS/perf/strace profiles and four
fully written-ring cells finish with exact reopen checks. Written NVMe repeats
also decline1373/1356→450/439ops/s, while block write/flush elapsed averages
increase~3×; written SATA stays near7100ops/s. This excludes allocation as the
whole cause but does not isolate drive firmware from the block queue.
W111 remains open; no drive settings or production defaults change.
[Evidence and limitations](../status/devel-nuc-closure-20261010.md).

**XFS mechanism observed:** separate writer-TID counts show roughly two log-force
calls per fdatasync on growing files on both devices; warmed rings show zero.
Host-wide counters closely match growth and remain small for rings. This is
metadata-journal work, not a count of drive flushes. Stable raw SATA controls
do not repair the earlier sustained EFS SATA slowdown; NVMe cache/firmware
attribution remains unproven. A production layout port needs safe reuse
semantics first. Current durability barriers are retained.

**Oct 10 matched three-node drive test:** same frozen `6b8f05acb484` engine,
20 minutes per drive, true three-voter groups, preserved regular cluster stopped.
NVMe first/final rates 31.83/10.80 files/s and pooled server Raft sync
2.465/6.993 ms; SATA 562.73/299.40 files/s and 0.150/0.319 ms. Both drives slow;
SATA late rates fluctuate. NVMe root telemetry during slow phase has no reported
thermal events/warnings (composite <=45.85°C, sensor2 <=61.85°C). SATA health is
unavailable. Large inbox refusals are not necessary: NVMe records only 35,
SATA 124, with zero loader errors, replica catch-up and 64 exact cold payload
checks per drive. Normal four-node service/both mounts restore and verify.
**W111 remains open:** isolate growing-file/XFS versus drive service latency;
NAND cache cause and hardware ceiling remain unproved. This compares these two
models/storage paths, one run each, not protocols in general.
[Report](../status/w97-three-drive-20261010.md).

**Oct 10 latest merged-code observation:** all 16 newly captured branch tips
integrate at `6b8f05acb484` and deploy to preserved NUC stores. A continuous
20-minute write / 10-minute drained pause / 20-minute same-worker resume creates
138,881 files with zero loader errors. First-minute rates 152.47 and 159.35
files/s fall to final-minute 52.85 and 48.05; corresponding NVMe flush means
rise from 1.33/1.34 to 3.65/3.66 ms. Rest restores the burst without restart,
but the decline repeats. n3 retains 75,109 sampled inbox refusals; all replicas
catch up. No root SSD health data arrives; cache occupancy/thermal cause and
hardware ceiling remain unproved. Native and unchanged-repeat full/fault gates
pass (POSIX 212/212, peer 64/64), but retain the earlier concurrent-append
30-second timeout. Defaults/diagnostics off are restored; 128 sampled exact
cold payload checks and live executable hashes pass. **Keep W111 open.**
Next isolate sustained durable-write latency with root NVMe health and matched
EFS-stopped/loaded growing-WAL versus preallocated-overwrite probes.
[Report](../status/w97-latest-nvme-20261010.md).

**Oct 10 NUC:** return control reproduces fast-then-slow rates at 10 ms.
NVMe host flush mean rises 2.38 to 3.70 ms while rates fall; an independent
low-load XFS overwrite+fdatasync probe with EFS stopped measures NVMe 1.12 ms
versus SATA 85.9 microseconds at QD1. This localizes persistence costs but does
not identify the drive/filesystem mechanism or prove a software/hardware ceiling.
Checkpoint-tail experiment gains throughput but fails append replay acceptance;
keep the default; this persistence investigation remains open as W111. [Report](../archive/status-20261011/w93-checkpoint-cadence-20261010.md).


**Action:** Repeat growing-file, preallocated and fully written-ring controls
with comparable initial device state, workload/build IDs and durable payloads.
Correlate writer sync distributions, XFS journal activity, block dispatch/
completion latency, queue depth and scheduler waits; record device health,
temperature and power/cache telemetry where available. Separate EFS-stopped
controls from loaded EFS tests and NVMe from SATA verdicts. Keep existing
durability barriers and normal service/data intact.

**Done when:** Repeated controls identify the dominant cause with evidence
that distinguishes filesystem, block-queue and device effects. Any proposed
repair must improve sustained rates/tails in repeated comparable NUC runs,
retain bounded queues and peer progress, and pass exact cold-byte, native,

**Related:** W97 replication feedback, W93 group commit, W96 KV WAL allocation, W53 mixed-write tails and W99 capacity policy.

### W113 · Aggregate application workload telemetry across FUSE clients

**Status:** proposed feature; implementation and live acceptance NOTRUN.
**Requested:** October 13, 2026. Initial target: ORCD, four storage nodes and
seven test clients. Documented on devel; no deployment or C changes authorized
by this note.

The portal should show the aggregate workload clients produce onto EFS,
separately from server storage activity, replication, erasure-coded fragments,
retries, background writeback and GC. Existing portal peaks select the largest
single-node sample; they are not simultaneous cluster or client totals.

**Recommended design:** inspect existing FUSE telemetry first. If it does not
expose application-boundary counters, add cumulative completed read/write
request counts and actual successful bytes returned/accepted at the FUSE
request/reply boundary. Record failures separately; optionally add metadata
operation counts. Do not count internal RPCs, retries or background flushes as
new application requests. Label writes as accepted application bytes, not
necessarily durably committed bytes. FUSE caching means these represent
requests reaching FUSE, not every userspace syscall or cached mmap access;
application benchmarking remains a separate measurement.

Expose per-mount identity, process/boot identity, monotonic sample time and
cumulative counters through a lightweight bounded interface. The portal polls
all configured test clients, derives rates from counter deltas and elapsed time,
and sums contemporaneous client samples by operation class. Handle restarts,
counter resets, multiple mounts, missing/stale samples and clock alignment
explicitly. Inspect existing interfaces before choosing a file or management
endpoint; the portal should not need to parse verbose logs.

**Display:** a minimal Client workload section with current aggregate read/write
ops/s and throughput, simultaneous peaks since portal start, peak timestamps
and coverage such as 7/7 clients reporting. Format bytes/s automatically as
B/s, KiB/s, MiB/s or GiB/s, with consistent IEC units. Keep Server storage I/O
and internal traffic separate. Sum the same interval's rates before recording a
peak; never add independently recorded per-client maxima. Mark incomplete
samples partial (for example 6/7) and exclude them from complete aggregate peaks.

**Acceptance:** deterministic counter/rate/format tests plus an ORCD seven-client
known-byte workload. Check exact successful/short/failed read/write accounting,
client restarts/resets, duplicate mount discovery, missing clients and peaks
occurring at different times. Demonstrate retries and replication do not inflate
client totals. Validate direct/TCP first; extend transport/mode coverage only if
the implementation touches those paths. No implementation or performance claim
is made by this discussion note.


### W115 · Storage-location availability and failure-domain inventory

**Status:** proposed feature; implementation/acceptance NOTRUN. Requested
October 13, 2026; initial ORCD topology: four nodes, six storage locations/node.
Documentation only; no failure injection, automatic repair or rollout.

Report stable storage identities, owning node, capacity, availability and last
observation for each location. Distinguish available, failed/unavailable,
read-only/unhealthy and unknown/stale; an up daemon does not prove all its paths
are working. Identify shared physical devices: 24 paths need not be 24 independent
failure domains. Keep location-count and capacity-weighted availability separate.

24/24 online is 100% location availability; 23/24 is 95.8%; losing one six-drive
node leaves 18/24 (75%). None of these is parity coverage or a safe-loss budget.
An unavailable drive/node is not necessarily permanently destroyed.

**Gates:** individual-drive failure with the node alive, whole-node outage,
missing/stale probes, duplicate device/path identities, unequal capacities and
recovery. Start with read-only reporting; fencing/re-placement policy remains
separate. Supplies observations to W116/W117; W99 still owns capacity protection.

### W116 · Verified byte-weighted data redundancy coverage

**Status:** proposed feature; implementation, physical inventory and live gates
NOTRUN. Node/capacity status and healing progress currently do not supply this
verified global percentage. Experimental repair prerequisites are not that metric.

Ordinary EFS 2+1 uses three fragment roles on three distinct nodes; any two valid
roles reconstruct a chunk. A fourth node adds placement capacity, not a second
parity role. Classify authoritative live logical payload bytes into:

- Fully protected: three accessible checksum-valid roles; one further role loss tolerable.
- Readable, degraded: two valid roles; no remaining fragment-loss margin.
- Unavailable: at most one valid role; not proof of permanent loss.
- Unknown/unverified: incomplete, stale or inconsistent authority/inventory.

Weight by logical payload bytes, not drives, file counts, physical fragment bytes
or nominal capacity. Define sparse-hole treatment and the denominator explicitly;
report verified versus total materialized live bytes. Include all required base,
delta and fold dependencies; a healthy base cannot hide a missing published delta.
Unused capacity is separate. Unknown bytes must not silently count as healthy.

Use bounded authoritative enumeration with a coherent generation/cut, physical
placement and integrity verification, durable store identities, scan progress and
observation age. Placement/liveness alone can supply only an explicitly labeled
estimate. Extra copies do not create extra independent roles. Revalidate after
concurrent publication/deletion/repair or root reincarnation; avoid unbounded RAM
and a full scrub on every portal poll. Do not imply automatic repair activation.

Keep data coverage separate from Raft quorum, service/read/write availability,
write admission, hardware health and repair progress. Metadata may be unavailable
while fragments remain reconstructable. No arbitrary percentage of drives is
safe to lose: two missing roles of the same chunk exceed its redundancy.

**Gates:** known-size fixtures with 3/2/1/0 roles, corrupt/missing roles, failed or
short probes, version races, duplicate copies, unequal root usage, sparse/overlay
content, restarts, partial scans and stale results. Byte categories must partition
the measured data correctly; restore protection only after verified durable
rebuild. Preserve W71/W75 and read-authority/repair contracts; none close here.

### W117 · Portal protection breakdown and failure-scenario comparison

**Status:** proposed feature/mockup; implementation/measured ORCD health NOTRUN.
Depends on W115/W116. Show separate storage availability and a compact pie/donut
of protected, readable-degraded, unavailable and unknown logical bytes. Include
percentages, human-friendly bytes, verified age and inventory coverage. Label
estimates versus verified measurements; keep metadata quorum and repair progress
separate. Do not present one overall health score or a safe-drive-loss allowance.

Illustrative pre-repair model only: four nodes, six equal independent drives/node,
uniform equal-byte groups on all three-of-four node placements and six drive
choices/node, all three roles initially valid. Not observed ORCD values:

| Failure | Drives online | Fully protected | Readable, degraded | Unavailable |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| None | 24/24 (100%) | 100% | 0% | 0% |
| One drive | 23/24 (95.8%) | 87.5% | 12.5% | 0% |
| Three drives on one node | 21/24 (87.5%) | 62.5% | 37.5% | 0% |
| One drive on each of three nodes | 21/24 (87.5%) | 66.55% | 29.51% | 3.94% |
| One node | 18/24 (75%) | 25% | 75% | 0% |
| Two nodes | 12/24 (50%) | 0% | 50% | 50% |

Reproduce by enumerating four three-node subsets and 6^3 root assignments each
(864 equal-weight groups). Fail drive indices below f[n], with vectors
[0,0,0,0], [1,0,0,0], [3,0,0,0], [1,1,1,0], [6,0,0,0], [6,6,0,0]; classify by
0/1/2-or-more missing roles. Actual placement, uneven usage, corruption,
incomplete third writes and rebuilds change the results. These are data-byte
coverage charts, not whole-file recovery or metadata/client availability.

**Gates:** deterministic model/chart calculations, byte/percentage formatting,
accessible labels, unknown/partial/stale inventories, identical drive counts with
different failure domains, and verified rebuild transitions. Measured ORCD
protection claims require W116 evidence first.

### W118 · Direct-read/fork application-buffer correctness

**Class/state:** Transport-independent platform correctness; historical ORCD
failure open, not reproduced on private Intel (Oct 14, 2026). Separate from
closed W100 and broader RDMA acceptance W106.

**Evidence:** Historical ORCD reads return stale application-buffer bytes when
another thread forks, despite correct bytes captured before FUSE replies.
Current private Intel uses matching devel production inputs with TCP/direct I/O,
`.efs` client/server and expiry disabled. The original
fork/no-fork controls pass. Intel's loaded FUSE module matches the inspected
on-disk build and uses direct-I/O page pin/unpin APIs. No kernel version-only
claim about ORCD vendor backports is justified.

when every fork fails, requires measured successful fork/read activity, checks
exact EOF and adds a child-held disjoint-prefix COW stress control. Native and
ASan/UBSan/leak self-tests pass on both Intel hosts, including corruption/length
negative controls; the native fork-failure interposer is correctly rejected.
Final qualification passes 281600 exact-byte/EOF cycles, mounted core 216/216
per host and fresh-client 4096-file/1 GiB verification per host. Production/private
main identities are unchanged; no extra client/test controller remains. This is
a test correction, not an EFS data-path repair.

**Remaining:** Inspect the loaded FUSE implementation on an actually failing
host and reproduce there with the strengthened oracle. If page pinning is
missing, qualify an appropriate vendor kernel fix/equivalent upstream
`738adade96b2` backport. Do not change cache-coherence behavior or label Intel's
non-reproduction as a universal fix. ORCD was not changed or requalified here.

**Qualification/reproduction:** [Private Intel fork/read ledger](../status/intel-direct-read-fork-20261014.md).
The ledger separates source-specific controls, final qualification, historical
failures and interrupted runs. W100 stays closed by human acceptance.

### W121 · Immediate read after successful fsync returns the previous file's payload

**Class/state:** normal-operation data correctness; OPEN, October16,2026.
On `fa29f9277` ORCD native RDMA/direct, `.efs` enabled,
expiry disabled: seven clients, eight writers and two query
threads each. Unique512-byte file: create/write/fsync/close, exact readback,
unlink. Four90s rounds reproduced255 mismatches in123,932 cycles, although
all write/fsync/close and unlink operations returned success. Both unmodified
devel and the restored queued-read-vote candidate fail; this is not isolated
to that scheduling change. Examples return the prior file's512-byte value.

**Diagnosis/gate, October 16:** correct bytes reach the FUSE reply, but
concurrent fork causes stale application buffers on ORCD's unpinned FUSE
kernel read path. Fixed-file reproduction: 86,629/433,368 failures with fork,
0/486,164 with posix_spawn. The installed module uses iov_iter_get_pages2;
upstream fix 738adade96b2 pins these pages. Kernel remediation is deferred
by the user; W121 remains OPEN. Isolate query subprocesses from reader
address spaces for performance experiments, without treating that workaround
as application correctness acceptance. Require a fixed-kernel fork/read
rerun plus original mixed load, peer and clean-restart checks.
[Diagnosis and regression](../status/orcd-w121-fork-read-20261016.md).
Unplanned recovery remains deferred.
[Reproduction, source identities and results](../status/orcd-queued-read-vote-20261016.md).

### W122 · Discoverable effective settings for efsd, efs-fuse and the portal

**Class/state:** product observability feature; PROPOSED, October 16, 2026.
Requested for the stable beta product. This item records the feature; backend
implementation and end-to-end acceptance are NOTRUN. It does not restore
archived experimental features or enable expiry.

**Problem:** binary help lists command-line options and efs-mgmt offers
individual status/policy commands, but there is no complete machine-readable
catalog of supported startup settings and runtime controls, or their effective
values. The portal's process argument/environment probe can show explicit
launch overrides only. An unset variable is not proof of a disabled feature;
version defaults, normalization and later policy changes remain invisible.
The current portal Settings draft is partial observability, not completion.

**Proposed behavior:**

- Maintain role-specific catalogs for `efsd` and `efs-fuse`, shared by help,
  validation and introspection where practical. Include CLI options, supported
  environment settings and existing mutable runtime policies. Do not expose
  fault-injection controls as supported beta configuration.
- Provide a versioned JSON interface, provisionally `efs-mgmt settings --json`,
  identifying the target process/role and build. Daemon lookup and FUSE-client
  lookup need distinct explicit targets: the daemon cannot infer client state.
  Define an authenticated/authorized read-only client introspection mechanism
  independent of whether `.efs` commands are enabled.
- For every supported setting report name, description, type, unit, valid
  range/choices, build-specific default, effective value, value source and
  applicability. Sources distinguish CLI, environment, default and runtime
  policy. Report restart/remount-required versus live-changeable, and identify
  any existing supported setter without adding a universal mutation endpoint.
- Read normalized active state rather than presenting environment text as
  effective configuration. Mark unavailable, unsupported, redacted and unset
  states distinctly. Never disclose credentials or arbitrary environment data.
- Near the bottom of the portal, show a read-only Settings section with a
  process selector, daemon/client scope, build identity and observation time.
  Distinguish stale/disconnected data and mixed builds. Keep a clearly labelled
  partial fallback for older binaries; never invent defaults for them.

**Acceptance gates:** catalog coverage of supported startup/runtime controls;
CLI/environment precedence and validation; defaults versus explicit overrides;
normalized/effective values; live policy updates; restart/remount semantics;
separate daemon and client targets; disabled `.efs`; access denial/redaction;
mixed/older builds; stale portal observations. Run focused integration on AMD
or Intel with a small cluster and two clients; ORCD scale is not required.
No live configuration editor or automatic rollout is included in this item.

### W123 — Automatic crash recovery through per-file durable versions

**New feature; proposed 2026-10-16.** Design/ordering review first; implementation and acceptance NOTRUN. Recover committed state without node format/rebuild while retaining immediate visibility, grouped barriers and fsync guarantees. Related W71 stays open. [Canonical feature plan and gates](../backlog/crash-safe-durable-versions.md).

<a id="w124"></a>
### W124 — Fast delete: quota at delete, batched reclaim and fragment slot reuse

**Performance/capacity; proposed 2026-10-18.** Design review first; implementation, private A/B and orcd-mini acceptance NOTRUN. POSIX delete stays metadata-only. Revised after design review: logical quota is credited exactly once when removal is final, with reclaim-pending bytes and physical availability (atomic per-filesystem reservations) reported separately. Reclaim moves from inode-at-a-time processing (2–3 proposals and ~8 fsyncs per inode) to bounded batches per owning group, with a journal-first node protocol (accepted for reclaim before the acknowledgement, physically reclaimed later). Rate targets are hypotheses for the A/B. Then small-file packing (W125). Slot reuse (needs reader retirement) and subtree delete are deferred. Motivated by 0.18–0.21 GiB/min reclaim and a 398 GiB-per-node backlog on orcd-mini. [Canonical proposal and gates](../backlog/fast-delete-reclaim.md).

<a id="w125"></a>
### W125 — Small-file packing by default (background packer)

**Capacity/performance; proposed 2026-10-18; revised to background packing after close.** Packing at close failed the early P1 measurement (close 5.4× slower, throughput −71 to −78%), so files are written exactly as today and an always-on background packer moves closed files below the threshold (initially 16 KiB) into shared segments of ordinary fragments (no data in metadata rows), lifetime-grouped by publication group, directory subtree and creation epoch, then retires their per-file fragments through W124's batched journal. Larger files keep per-file fragments. The same copy-forward engine compacts survivors of mostly-dead segments (bounded overhead ≤1/t). One write path and no switch that disables the packer: tag the last devel commit without it (`archive/unpacked-small-files-<date>`); comparisons build the tag. Existing small files are backfilled. Pieces ported from `archive/packing-containers-20261016` (D37) without the client writer, cohorts, `EFS_PACKED_WRITES` or the container engine. Motivated by ~800× raw amplification for sub-KiB files on orcd-mini. [Canonical proposal and gates](../backlog/small-file-packing-default.md) · [implementation plan](../backlog/small-file-packing-plan.md).

<a id="w126"></a>
### W126 — KV readers convoy behind exclusive LSM phases on a busy leader

**Performance; opened 2026-10-21. Steps 1 and 3 deployed on orcd-mini (`8fb4247ad`, 2026-10-21 23:14Z). Lock-wait gate PASS; create-rate gate FAIL (no measurable gain; throughput is bounded elsewhere). Step 4 deferred.** [A/B evidence](../status/orcd-mini-w126-ab-8fb4247ad-20261022.md).
Found under the user's 32M-file `tiny_files.py` run on orcd-mini `47ba6b590`
([profile](../status/orcd-mini-profile-47ba6b590-20261021.md)). From ~1.0 to
~2.6 M files, creates fell from 2,564 to 1,130 files/s. Over the same span,
leader n1's LSM lock waits rose from 3.3% to 16–18% of its context switches.
- About 93% of the read waits were LOOKUP → `efs_meta_apply_getattr` gets.
- Apply's own blocked switches sat in `pthread_rwlock_wrlock`: 1,051 in a
  3 s DWARF capture.
- `apply-sleep` (>20 ms) occurred 1,400–2,600 times per ~90 s window, up to
  400 ms.

**Mechanism.** Every KV read (point get or scan) shares one `view_rw` per
node. The lock is writer-preferring so Raft apply cannot starve. Each
exclusive acquisition (`lsm_lock`) therefore waits for every in-flight
reader, including long scans, and new readers queue behind it. Both Raft
groups share the node's KV, so W66's leader distribution alone does not
remove this ([`h->mu` plan](../status/raft-host-mu-plan-20261016.md)).

**Step 1 (implemented).** Writer-owned flags and counters change only under
`mu`, and readers only read them. A new `lsm_peek_lock` takes `mu` without
`view_rw` for read-only peeks:
- the failure-flag check before every batch's WAL append, which halves the
  exclusive phases per applied batch;
- REPORT's `efs_kv_lsm_l0_hot`;
- `efs_kv_lsm_stats` and `seg_count`;
- the query-refresh revision reads (`metadata_revisions`,
  `transaction_revision`/`activity`, `cleanup_deferred`).

Peeks kept `lsm_lock`'s fail-fast abort inside a read section (removed
by the October 24 peek-ordering fix below).
`tests/test_kv_lsm.c` `test_peek_beside_reader` parks a reader inside a scan
callback and requires every peek to return. It FAILs on `47ba6b590` and
PASSes with the change. On node9901, the patched tree passes `test_kv_lsm`,
`test_kv_lsm_concurrent 4`, `test_kv`, `test_meta_apply`, `test_raft_store`,
`test_query_disk`, `test_txn`, `test_kv_snapshot_tail`, `test_kv_reader_gate`
and `test_query_catalog`.

**Step 2 (folded into step 3).** A flush of 100 ms or more logs
`kv-flush: files= io_ms= manifest_ms= view_yielded=`. On orcd-mini, flushes
wrote 26–37 L0 files with 117–160 ms of I/O each. Before step 3, all of that
ran under the exclusive view.

**Step 3 (`8fb4247ad`, implemented and deployed).** After the pending merge
the memtable is frozen, because every writer waits on `mu`. At the outermost
writer level, `kv_flush_locked` therefore yields the exclusive view and keeps
`mu` while it writes and fsyncs the L0 files, the MANIFEST and the WAL
reset. It retakes the view only to publish the L0 slots and to clear the
memtable. Between those two steps, readers find identical rows in both. The
memtable still clears only after the MANIFEST write succeeds.
`test_kv_lsm` and three runs of `test_kv_lsm_concurrent 8` PASS.

**Verification.**
- `make test` (`scripts/make_test_summary.sh`): 813/813 commands, 1
  environmental failure (docs check without `results/`).
- orcd-mini deploy and POSIX smoke: 216/216 PASS.
- A/B (A 8fb, B 47ba, A' 8fb) with the user's exact `tiny_files.py` shape,
  at matched new-file counts:
  - leader LSM lock waits 1.6–6.0% vs 13.6% at 0.9 M, and 5.4% vs 20.9% at
    1.7 M;
  - creates/s 736 / 598 / 551 at 0.9 M, which follows the run order, not
    the build.

The remaining leader waits are `h->mu` in `host_pump`, proposals and REPORT
([`h->mu` plan](../status/raft-host-mu-plan-20261016.md)), plus XFS log
fsync waits.

**Peek ordering (October 24, `680a7d0dd` on
`claude/devel-w126-peek-8a1155`, not merged).** K30 pinned a remaining
defect: peeks took `mu`, and a writer holds `mu` while it waits on
`view_rw` for readers, so every peek waited for the longest reader. Peeks
now take a separate `peek_mu`, which a writer holds exactly while it owns
`view_rw` exclusively (order `mu`, `view_rw`, `peek_mu`). Yield, reclaim
and cond waits release and retake it with the view, so peeks also run
during flush I/O. A peek inside a read section is now allowed.
`test_peek_beside_reader` is a liveness test in four modes, and there are
new peek storms beside flushes and compactions. `make leak-check` no
longer skips the case. [Evidence](../status/w126-peek-order-20261024.md);
the orcd-mini A/B rerun is NOTRUN.

**Remaining.** Step 4 (bound how long `merge_scan` holds the shared view) is
deferred until LSM waits rise again. Create throughput on orcd-mini is not
a W126 matter.

<a id="w127-w131-fix"></a>
### W127–W131 apply hardening — implementation (October 22)

**Implemented on `claude/dead-code-cleanup-5f7087`; not merged.** One package,
as the scope review asked:
- `EFS_ERR_UNSUPPORTED` (-24) is the "unsupported or malformed encoding"
  class. Dispatch returns it for unknown tags and for reserved or retired
  tags; the DIR, SESSION and TXN decoders for unknown sub-tags and short
  frames; the other decoders for length and count errors. No normalization
  list in `host_apply` turns it into success. Business refusals (SALT
  mismatch, QUERY_POLICY CAS, the other ring verdicts) are unchanged, and
  group-routing mismatches still answer INVAL/PROTO.
- On that result `host_apply` aborts the KV scope (no cursor), returns the
  error so the Raft core does not advance `applied`, and marks the group
  `incompatible` (sticky, separate from `kv_incomplete`): one diagnostic
  line with group, index, term, tag, sub-tag and length; step-down; no
  campaign; proposals and ReadIndex refused with `EFS_ERR_UNSUPPORTED`.
  A retried apply returns at once without dispatching.
- W130: DIR returns IO/NOMEM so the per-index retry applies.
- W131: no KV engine returns IO (logged once) instead of OK; the empty
  no-op entry still applies.

**Evidence (node9901, gcc 11.5.0):**
- `tests/test_apply_unsupported.py` (wired): the production `host_apply`
  over a real KV LSM. An unsupported verdict on a normally-normalized tag
  leaves no row and no cursor, also after reopening the KV; the state is
  sticky; another group on the same KV still applies; a missing engine is
  refused; DIR storage errors retry; unknown or short DIR/TXN frames are
  unsupported. `test_gc_verdict.py` checks that no verdict list absorbs it.
- `scripts/w127_incompatible_entry.sh`: a private 3-node TCP efsd set
  (ports 17631–17633). An entry with unknown tag 200 is committed to
  group 0; all replicas log the diagnostic and keep `applied` below it;
  group 0 has no leader and refuses a new MKFS; group 2 keeps its leader
  and stays applied; after restarting all nodes the same holds. PASS.

**Remaining:** RDMA and multi-host runs; the one-replica DIR fault
injection (W130); cross-group and cached read refusal and a status-reply
field (W66 B4); prevalidating batch members before the first side effect
(they are rejected inside the aborted scope today). **New finding:** the
proposal RPC accepts a tag this build does not know, so any connection can
commit such an entry and halt a group. Submit-side refusal of unknown tags
belongs with the W133 connection-state matrix.

<a id="w127"></a>
### W127 — Metadata apply accepts unknown command tags as applied

**Correctness; opened 2026-10-21 from the [dead-code audit](../reviews/dead-code-review-20261021.md) M1; FIXED on `claude/dead-code-cleanup-5f7087` (not merged); unit and private 3-node gates PASS, RDMA/multi-host NOTRUN.**
`host_apply_dispatch` ends in `return EFS_OK;` (`src/server/raft_host.c:3507`).
Only the reserved ranges 45–51 and 55–57 are refused (`:3410–3416`). Any other
tag this build does not know is consumed: the KV cursor advances
(`:3005–3010`), and `applied` moves past the entry on every replica, with no
effect and no error. Evidence is a code reading at `0bdf55256`, confirmed by an
independent review. It has not been triggered on a cluster.

**Fix and gate:** this is the concrete defect behind [W66](../status/metadata-scaling.md#w66-acceptance-checklist-consolidated-oct-21)
B1–B4.
- Add a distinct fatal "unsupported encoding" outcome, decided before any
  mutation.
- On that outcome: abort the KV scope, leave the cursor and `applied`
  unchanged, and withdraw readiness.
- Test at the real apply boundary with a synthetic unknown tag: check the
  verdict, the cursor, and the state after restart.
- No old-binary or old-log matrix.

<a id="w128"></a>
### W128 — Metadata apply accepts unknown sub-tags and short frames as applied

**Correctness; opened 2026-10-21 from the audit M2; FIXED on `claude/dead-code-cleanup-5f7087` (not merged); unit gates PASS.**
These decoders return `EFS_OK` without any effect (`raft_host.c`):
- `apply_dir_cmd`: short frame (`:2226–2227`) and unknown kind (`:2239–2240`).
- `apply_session_cmd`: short header (`:2381–2382`), per-kind short frames
  (`:2387`, `:2393`, `:2404`, `:2430`, `:2454`, `:2474`, `:2482`, `:2511`)
  and `default:` (`:2515–2516`).
- `apply_txn_cmd`: `default:` (`:2834–2835`).

Evidence: code reading at `0bdf55256`; not triggered on a cluster.

**Fix and gate:** route these cases to the W127 outcome. W66 B1 names "every
sub-tag". Validate every member of a batch before any side effect. Test with
synthetic malformed frames for each decoder.

<a id="w129"></a>
### W129 — `host_apply` turns decoder errors into success and commits the cursor

**Correctness; opened 2026-10-21 from the audit M3; FIXED on `claude/dead-code-cleanup-5f7087` (not merged); unit gates PASS.**
- For about 45 command tags (`raft_host.c:2941–2962`), `host_apply` forces
  the result to `EFS_OK` whatever the apply returned. Only IO/NOMEM are
  restored (`:2984–3000`).
- So a decoder `EFS_ERR_PROTO` (for example a wrong-length CREATE) commits
  the cursor and is skipped on every replica.
- QUERY_POLICY (`:2966`), CREATE_REFUSAL/EXPIRY (`:2967–2970`) and nine
  SESSION sub-tags (`:2975–2982`) do the same.
- `tests/test_gc_verdict.py:75` asserts
  `core_result(EFS_MD_CMD_APPEND_RES,EFS_ERR_PROTO,37)==EFS_OK`, so the test
  suite currently protects this behaviour.

**Not every PROTO is a decode failure.** SALT answers PROTO for an anchor
mismatch (`:2933–2935`), and QUERY_POLICY treats PROTO as a logical CAS
verdict (`:2963–2966`). Both are legitimate business refusals.

**Fix and gate:**
- Decoders return the W127 malformed/unsupported outcome. Business refusals,
  PROTO included where it means a refusal, stay ring verdicts.
- Removing PROTO from one allow-list is not the fix.
- Replace the expression-level check in `test_gc_verdict.py` with tests at
  the apply boundary: verdict, cursor and restart.

<a id="w130"></a>
### W130 — DIR apply swallows storage errors; replicas can diverge

**Correctness; opened 2026-10-21 from the audit M4; FIXED on `claude/dead-code-cleanup-5f7087` (not merged); decoder unit gate PASS, one-replica fault-injection gate NOTRUN.**
- `apply_dir_cmd` maps NOT_FOUND/INVAL/BUSY to OK, then logs every other rc
  (IO and NOMEM included) and returns `EFS_OK` (`raft_host.c:2242–2249`).
- DIR is also missing from the IO-retry list (`:2984–3000`).
- A failed directory split or migrate step therefore advances the cursor on
  that replica only. The size-triggered split is live
  (`src/meta/dir_layout.c:23–37`).

Evidence: code reading at `0bdf55256`; not triggered on a cluster.

**Fix and gate:**
- Return IO/NOMEM so the existing per-index retry applies.
- Route malformed DIR entries to W127.
- Test: inject a DIR storage failure on one replica, then show recovery and
  equal state on all replicas.
- If the spread-policy decision removes this path (audit X1), close W130
  with that removal.

<a id="w131"></a>
### W131 — Missing KV engine counts as applied

**Correctness; opened 2026-10-21 from the audit M5; FIXED on `claude/dead-code-cleanup-5f7087` (not merged); unit gate PASS, reachability still unproven.**
`host_apply` stamps the apply ring `EFS_OK` and returns OK when
`!h || !h->kv || !cmd || clen==0` (`raft_host.c:2891–2896`). `clen==0` (a
Raft no-op) is legitimate. A missing `h->kv` is not: the entry would be
consumed without effect. No path that reaches it with the pump running is
known yet, so confidence is Medium.

**Fix and gate:** separate the no-op case from the missing-engine case, and
make a missing engine fatal. A unit test of `host_apply` with no KV engine
must leave the cursor unchanged.

<a id="w132"></a>
### W132 — `NODE_LEFT` lets any connection drop a node from membership

**Correctness / safety; opened 2026-10-21 from the audit P3; FIXED on
branch `devel-k03` (`8727e3afe`, 2026-10-22), unit gate PASS, cluster
NOTRUN.**
- Fix: ID 24 is retired and listed in `EFS_MSG_IS_RETIRED`, so a frame
  carrying it is refused before dispatch by `retired_refuse` (no reply,
  connection closed). The `NODE_LEFT` case in `handler.c`, `struct
  efs_msg_node_left` and `server_remove_node_from_cluster` (no other
  caller) are deleted. No ID moves; no replacement message.
- Gate: `tests/test_node_left_refused.py` (in `make test`) embeds the real
  receive-and-refusal prefix of `server_handle_conn`, sends a `NODE_LEFT`
  frame over a socketpair and checks no reply, closed connection, nothing
  dispatched, membership unchanged; a `HEARTBEAT` control frame proves the
  embedded loop dispatches live frames. `tests/test_retired_messages.py`
  lists 24. Build PASS on efs2 (Fedora 42, aarch64, gcc); every `make test`
  line PASS there except `./tests/test_reclaim`, which fails the same way
  on a pristine devel build of the same host (hardcoded `/tmp` roots on a
  972 MB tmpfs) and is unrelated; the live wrapper test needs `TMPDIR` on
  a real disk for the same reason. Not exercised against a running cluster.
- `src/server/handler.c:902–911` calls `server_remove_node_from_cluster`
  (`src/server/cluster.c:402`) for any connection that sends
  `EFS_MSG_NODE_LEFT`. It needs no declaration and no peer identity.
- Nothing in the tree sends this message (`git grep -w EFS_MSG_NODE_LEFT`).
- Evidence is a code reading, confirmed by review. It was not exercised
  against a server.

**Fix and gate:**
- Delete the handler and refuse the message ID explicitly. Membership
  changes go through Raft.
- Test: a synthetic `NODE_LEFT` gets a refusal and leaves membership
  unchanged.
- This is a narrow fix. It does not authenticate other requests (W133).

<a id="w133"></a>
### W133 — Client protocol declaration gate is fail-open

**Correctness; opened 2026-10-21 from the audit P1; OPEN, fix NOTRUN.**
- Only `INODE_GETCHUNKS`, `GET_SEGMENT` and `PUT_SEGMENT` require
  `CLIENT_HELLO` (`handler.c:186–190`).
- Every other request (`PUT_CHUNK`, namespace mutations, REPORT, …) is served
  on an undeclared connection.
- The version check is `>= EFS_PROTOCOL_MIN_VERSION` (`handler.c:196`,
  `src/common/protocol.c:697`), so newer versions are accepted too.
- `scripts/w125_p3_compat.sh` case 2 expects an old client's writes to keep
  working, which contradicts the no-backward-compatibility rule.

**Fix and gate:**
- Require one exact supported declaration, defined as a connection-state and
  message matrix: client, peer (HELLO) and management connections have
  different valid operations, and the declaration messages themselves must be
  accepted.
- Cover TCP and RDMA, reconnects and forwarding connections.
- Test with synthetic unsupported and missing declarations.
- Turn `w125_p3_compat.sh` into a refusal test or delete it.
- A declaration is not authentication, and this item does not claim it.

<a id="w133-fix"></a>
**Implementation (October 22, branch `devel-k04`, not merged):**
- `EFS_PROTOCOL_VERSION` is 3, and `EFS_PROTOCOL_MIN_VERSION` is removed.
  Both sides require an exact match. A client also refuses a server that
  accepts it with another version.
- `efs_decl_gate_frame` (`src/common/protocol.c`) runs on every frame in
  `server_handle_conn` before dispatch, on TCP and RDMA alike. Before an
  accepted CLIENT_HELLO only HEARTBEAT is served. Any other request is
  refused with no reply, the connection is closed, and one rate-limited
  `handler: refused ...` line is logged.
- A mismatched declaration gets `{EFS_ERR_PROTO, 3}` and the connection is
  closed. This also applies on an already-declared connection.
- Every efsd connection opener declares first:
  - **efs-fuse:** the pool declares before the RDMA upgrade. Discovery
    (LIST_NODES) and the mount bootstrap (RAFT_STATUS) declare too.
  - **Daemon peer pool:** declares before the RDMA upgrade and before the
    HELLO/build-id join gate. Joins, Raft and forwards all use this pool.
  - **efs-mgmt:** every command uses `efs_connect_declared`. The status
    probe declares under its own 2 s bound.
  - **Tests:** the live and measure C programs, the raw-socket Python live
    tests and `scripts/w127_incompatible_entry.sh` all declare.
- These openers are exempt:
  - Reachability probes in `node_cache.c` connect and close without
    sending anything.
  - `tests/perf/tcp_rdma/xprt_bench` and the self-hosted unit tests
    (`test_rdma_xprt`, `test_rdma_segmented`, `test_data`) are their own
    server, not efsd.
- `scripts/w125_p3_compat.sh` now expects old clients to be refused and
  exits nonzero otherwise.
- **Gates:**
  - `tests/test_declaration_gate.c` PASS on efs3 (TCP frame path). It
    covers undeclared requests refused without a reply, HEARTBEAT, wrong,
    short and bad-magic declarations, an accepted declaration followed by
    a served request, and client-side refusal.
  - `tests/test_declaration_gate_handler.py` PASS. It checks the handler
    ordering and that every opener declares.
  - The RDMA frame path of the same test is NOTRUN on efs3 (no IB device).
  - `make test` on efs3 (Fedora 42, aarch64, TMPDIR on disk), every
    command run independently: 874 of 875 PASS. The one failure,
    `tests/test_reclaim` (`t_basic` put assertion), fails identically on
    devel `19555889f` on efs3, so this branch did not cause it.
  - Fake-server and handler-slice tests now answer or stub the declaration
    (`test_gc_status_expiry.py`, `test_expiry_cli.py`,
    `test_node_left_refused.py`).
  - The cluster refusal run (`w125_p3_compat.sh`) is NOTRUN.

<a id="w135"></a>
### W135 — A plain `make test` stops at the docs gate before the code tests

**Test reporting; opened 2026-10-21 from the audit T1; FIXED on `devel-k25` (October 22), gate run on efs3 below.**
- `python3 docs/check-architecture.py` was a command in the middle of the
  `test` recipe (`Makefile:455` at `0bdf55256`).
- On `0bdf55256` it failed `regen-diff` (a status README edit without
  regeneration), so 162 of the 276 recipe commands never ran, including every
  `./tests/test_*` unit binary.
- With the docs regenerated in a private copy, `make test` passed on node9901
  (rc=0, 2 min 29 s).
- The current devel docs are regenerated (gate 5/5), but the structure still
  lets any docs lag stop a plain `make test` before the code tests.
- Scope correction (October 21): the node9901 verdict runner
  `scripts/make_test_summary.sh` (`0e9df00a8`) already runs every `make test`
  command independently and continues past failures. Code results are lost
  only when `make test` is run directly, as the audit did, so this is a
  reporting gap, not a hidden verdict.

**Fix and gate:**
- Split `test` into independent docs and code targets that both always run,
  or document `make_test_summary.sh` as the only qualifying runner.
- `test` reports a nonzero aggregate if either fails.
- Moving the line, or making it a prerequisite, does not help: a failing
  prerequisite also stops the recipe.

**Fix (October 22, `devel-k25`, alpha K25):**
- The docs gate is out of the `test` recipe. It stays `make docs-check`;
  the new `make check` runs `test` and `docs-check` each to completion and
  exits nonzero if either failed. The gate itself is unchanged.
- A second reason, found while fixing: the link check resolves into
  `results/`, which release trees and archived copies omit, so the gate
  failed every `make test` on a node tree (see the orcd-mini deploy and
  tiny-profile pages). The code gate no longer depends on `results/`.
- Regression check: `tests/test_make_test_recipe.py` (in `make test`)
  parses `make -n test` and fails if any command names the docs gate.
- `scripts/make_test_summary.sh` is unchanged: it runs the `test` recipe's
  commands, which are now the code tests only. Run `make docs-check` where
  the docs and `results/` exist (the Mac checkout).
- Gate: `make test` on efs3 and `make docs-check` on the Mac, recorded in
  the K25 report.

  `'atomic_thread_fence' is not supported with '-fsanitize=thread' [-Werror=tsan]`
  (`src/server/apply_ring.h:38`, `:61`).
- The test prints `SKIP` and passes (`tests/test_apply_ring.py:229–231`), so
  the race check and its negative control never run on the build node.

**Fix and gate:** fix the test, not the synchronization.
- The ring payload already uses atomics, and the fences carry the seqlock
  ordering.
- `-Wno-error=tsan` can enable a diagnostic run, but TSan does not model the
  fences, so a clean run is not proof.
- Keep the torn-record stress check and the negative control, record the
  sanitizer's limits, and report SKIP as NOTRUN.
- Any change to the memory ordering needs its own correctness review.

**Fix (October 22, `devel-k25`, alpha K25), test only, no change to
`apply_ring.h`:**
- The TSan half runs or the test fails with the reason; there is no SKIP
  path left. A build failure (including a missing `libtsan`) and a binary
  that does not run both exit nonzero with the compiler or runtime output.
- gcc's `'atomic_thread_fence' is not supported with '-fsanitize=thread'`
  is allowed with `-Wno-error=tsan` for the sanitizer build only, and only
  after the plain build reported it (clang does not); the fences stay.
- The limit is in the PASS line: TSan does not model the fences, so a
  clean run covers the atomic payload accesses, not the ordering; the
  torn-record stress check (4 M native writes, 3 readers, 0 torn) is the
  ordering gate. The TSan builds use 400 k writes. The plain-field negative
  control still runs and must be reported as a data race.
- Verified: Mac/clang PASS; efs3 gcc 15.0.1 aarch64 PASS after
  `libtsan` was installed there (the gcc build without the retry does
  fail `-Werror=tsan`, so the retry path is exercised). node9901 gcc 11:
  NOTRUN here, expected to take the same path.

<a id="w140"></a>
### W140 — The proposal RPC accepts metadata tags this build cannot apply

**Correctness / safety; opened 2026-10-22 from the W127 gate; fix on
`devel-k02` (`8b8048a5b`), unit gates PASS on efs1; cluster gate NOTRUN.**
- `EFS_MSG_RAFT_MKFS` with a payload (`server_raft_host_submit`) refuses
  only reserved and retired tags (`EFS_MD_CMD_IS_RESERVED`). Any other byte
  is proposed and committed.
- Since W127, every replica refuses such an entry at apply and the group
  stops serving until it is reformatted. So one request from any connection
  can halt a metadata group.
- Shown by `scripts/w127_incompatible_entry.sh` on node9901 (tag 200 to
  group 0, October 22).

**Fix (`8b8048a5b`, October 22):**
- `include/efs/meta_cmd.h` carries `EFS_MD_CMD_APPLIED`, the table of log
  commands this build applies, and `efs_md_cmd_applicable()`. It is the one
  source of truth: `host_apply_dispatch` checks it before any handler (the
  final `EFS_ERR_UNSUPPORTED` halt stays for anything a handler cannot
  decode), and `host_tag_refused()` refuses every other tag with
  `EFS_ERR_PROTO` at the top of `host_propose_impl`, the only function that
  appends to a Raft log. The submit RPC, the inode RPC handlers, background
  reclaim, the packer (`server_raft_host_pack_propose`) and forwarded
  commands all end there. One log line per second, with the count of
  refusals suppressed in between.
- `tests/test_submit_unknown_tag.py` (in `make test`): the dispatcher
  compares against exactly the table's 48 tags, every log append is behind
  the gate, the predicate over all 256 values, and the production gate in
  front of a real single-voter Raft log: tag 200 (and reserved, retired,
  RPC-only and CFG tags) answer PROTO with the log and applied count
  unchanged, the next CREATE commits at the next index, the log line is
  rate-limited. `tests/test_meta_cmd_namespace.py` checks the table names
  every `EFS_MD_CMD_*` but host-only CFG and no `EFS_MD_REQ_*`.

**Remaining gate:**
- Cluster: tag 200 to group 0 through the proposal RPC answers PROTO, the
  group's log and applied index do not move, and the group keeps serving.
  `scripts/w127_incompatible_entry.sh` can no longer plant an incompatible
  entry through the RPC; the W127 B1-B4 gate needs another vehicle (a log
  entry written below the gate) before it is rerun.
- Who may submit at all is W133 (connection-state matrix); this item only
  closes the encoding hole.

<a id="w141"></a>
### W141 — `test_reclaim` "fail closed, recover, re-admit" fails under suite load

**Verification flake; opened 2026-10-22; FIXED on `devel-k25` (October 22), 20-run gate NOTRUN.**
- `t_fail_closed` waited at most 5 s (200 × 25 ms) for background journal
  recovery to clear `reclaim_fail_closed`.
- Under the full `make_test_summary.sh` run on node9901 it failed once in
  `dcclean-b4a` (October 21). Ten direct reruns in the same tree passed, and
  the other summary runs on the branch passed it.

**Fix and gate:** make the wait follow recovery progress (or a documented
larger bound), not a fixed 5 s; then 20 summary runs without a failure.

**Fix (October 22, `devel-k25`, alpha K25):** `wait_readmitted` in
`tests/test_reclaim.c` polls every 10 ms and follows the recovery
counters (`recovering`, `recovered` from `server_reclaim_status`): it
gives up only after 30 s without a change in them, or at a 300 s cap,
and prints the status when it does. A loaded host slows the export walk
without failing the test; a stalled recovery still fails with its
counters. Gate: 20 `make_test_summary.sh` runs on node9901 NOTRUN here.
- The test also put its storage roots under a fixed `/tmp`, ignoring
  `TMPDIR`. On efs3 `/tmp` is a tmpfs of about 1 GB, smaller than the
  physical guard's floor (max(5%, 1 GiB) + 256 MiB). So every PUT was
  refused (QUOTA) and the binary aborted in its first case, before the
  W141 case ran (devel fails the same way there). The roots now follow
  `TMPDIR`, which `make_test_summary.sh` sets to a disk path.
- efs3 result (October 22): the W141 case passed in 9 of 9 runs. The full
  binary passed 3 times, then the later "PUT racing acceptance" case got
  QUOTA as the 10 GB VM disk filled (its writer runs until stopped). That
  is a capacity limit of the VM, not this item; node9901 has the disk.

<a id="w127-w139-review"></a>
### Review of W127–W139 scope and priority — October 21

**All 13 items are worth tracking; they are not 13 demonstrated product bugs.**
Review of the items introduced by `e681ff97e`; documentation only, no fixes or
new runtime qualification. Existing OPEN/NOTRUN verdicts remain unchanged.

| Items | Assessment |
| --- | --- |
| W127–W130 | Confirmed unsafe apply behavior by code inspection. Preserve legitimate business refusals while fixing malformed-command and storage-error handling; cluster reproduction gates remain NOTRUN. |
| W131 | Defensive hardening with runtime reachability unproven, not a demonstrated running-cluster failure. |
| W132–W133 | Confirmed unsafe endpoint and protocol-enforcement gaps; declaration is not authentication. |
| W134 | Valid session-fencing gap, to be fixed together with registration of current mutation paths under W72. |
| W135 | Test-reporting improvement. Fail-fast is normal behavior; incomplete execution must not be presented as full qualification. Independent suite results should preserve an aggregate failure. |
| W136–W137 | Broken test fixtures, not evidence that the corresponding product behavior is wrong. Fix or remove with their associated functionality. |
| W138–W139 | Qualification gaps scoped to the audited environment/default suite. Absence from that suite does not mean a test cannot run manually or through a dedicated target. |

Keep the separate W numbers for traceability, but implement W127–W131 as one
coherent apply-hardening package with shared error classification and real
apply-boundary tests. W132 can proceed independently. W133 requires the
connection-state matrix; W134 requires the W72 integration, not an isolated
removal of its bypass.

Do not assign identical release-blocker status to all 13. Prioritize live
correctness/enforcement issues and trustworthy qualification of enabled paths.
Staged-feature tests may be removed when that feature is archived coherently;
this must not remove coverage of a still-exposed server endpoint. Qualification
must distinguish PASS, FAIL and NOTRUN, including environment-dependent checks.
Any release decision still needs the named acceptance results; this review does
not waive gates, close items, or authorize a release. No additional conceptual
review is needed before implementation against these requirements.

**Response (October 21).** Accepted. Two corrections on my side:
- W135 overstated its effect. `scripts/make_test_summary.sh`, the node9901
  verdict runner, continues past failures. Only a direct `make test` stops
  at the docs gate. W135 is renamed and its class narrowed to test
  reporting.
- The work-queue rows now show W131 as defensive hardening, and W127–W131
  as one apply-hardening package.

This review was a subsection of W139, which made it read as part of W139. It
is now its own section, with its text unchanged. No item is closed, and no
gate changes.

<a id="w143"></a>
### W143 — efs-fuse reads diagnostic environment switches on per-op paths

**Performance; opened and closed 2026-10-22 (both gates recorded); deployed in `46496416e`. Verified: `getenv` is gone from both clients' on-CPU profiles under the same load. `make test` 816/816 with one environmental failure (docs check without `results/`).**
Found by passively profiling orcd-mini on `08cc16af4` under two
`tiny_files.py` writers ([profile](../status/orcd-mini-profile-08cc16af4-20261022.md)).
On the node9901 client, `getenv` was 2.9% self and 3.7% with children of
efs-fuse on-CPU time. `__strncmp_evex` and `__strlen_evex`, used by
`getenv`'s environment scan, added another 1.8% and 1.1%. On node9900 it
was 1.3% on 2026-10-21. `getenv` walks the whole process environment on
every call. These checks read diagnostic switches that never change after
start:
- `EFS_RPC_PROF` in `dir_lock_take`: every directory lock, and 64 times
  per `efs_client_lock_all_dirs` (once per stripe) on the eviction path;
- `EFS_RPC_PROF` in `lookup_memo_observe` (every lookup) and
  `efs_append_flush_report_run` (every flush);
- `EFS_OPID_TRACE_VERBOSE` and `EFS_OPID_TRACE` in `inode_rpc.c`: several
  per create, lease and append;
- `EFS_STAGE_DBG` per eviction pass.

**Fix.** Each of the 20 affected functions reads its switch once into a
function-local `static int` (`-1` until read), as `write.c` already does
for `EFS_REPORT_DBG`. The cache stays inside the function: source-slice
tests compile these functions alone, and an earlier version that used a
shared header helper and file-scope caches broke 14 of them. Unchanged:
startup-only reads, error-path `EFS_RDMA_FIRST` logging and
`EFS_FAULTS`-only checks. Behaviour is unchanged, because no test or tool
sets these variables at runtime.

**Gates.**
- `make test` on node9901 (`scripts/make_test_summary.sh`). Many tests
  compile slices of the changed files.
- A client on-CPU profile under the same tiny-file load shows `getenv`
  below 0.1%.

The client is not the throughput limit here: both mounts used only
0.16–0.18 cores. The gain is efs-fuse CPU, not create rate.

<a id="w144"></a>
### W144 — LOOKUP/GETATTR on a group follower takes `h->mu` for the leader hint

**Performance; opened and closed 2026-10-22 (both gates recorded); deployed in `784bcc6ee`. Verified with split leadership (n3 led group 0, n2 led group 2): `host_namespace_leader_hint` no longer appears in the leaders' lock waits. `make test` 816/816 with one environmental failure.**
Found in the orcd-mini profile on `46496416e`
([profile, p2](../status/orcd-mini-profile-08cc16af4-20261022.md)). There,
leadership was split: n2 led group 0 and n1 led group 2. On n1,
`host_namespace_leader_hint` ← `host_read_leader_hint` ←
`server_raft_host_lookup` was the largest lock-wait site: 22.1% of n1's
lock-wait switches, ahead of proposals.

The function routes LOOKUP, GETATTR and namespace mutations to a dual-group
leader. When this node is not the group's leader, it took `h->mu` to read
both groups' committed voters. The 2026-10-18 profile saw nothing, because
then one node led both groups and the leader returns before locking.

**Fix.** Read the voters with `host_route_voters`, the lock-free published
view also used by `host_leader_cover_pick`: the raft voters for a hosted
group, else the slot's atomically stored set. A group without a local slot
still yields no hint, as before. The hint can be one pump cycle old, which
was already true, and the recipient rechecks authority.
`tests/test_namespace_leader_route.py` gets the matching stub; all its
assertions are unchanged and PASS. `test_host_cover_route` and
`test_query_target_route` PASS.

**Gates.**
- `make test` on node9901.
- After deploy, with split leadership, `host_namespace_leader_hint` is gone
  from the leader-node lock waits. One node leading both groups does not
  exercise the path.

<a id="w145"></a>
### W145 — A follower commits its own unproven log tail after an InstallSnapshot

**Raft safety; opened 2026-10-22. Root cause fixed and deployed (`76614e8e8`); orcd-mini n2 repaired 16:20Z with `efs-mgmt raft-resync`. The four remaining parts are fixed or answered on branch `devel-k01` (no client was acknowledged for 30,929,219@62); orcd-mini deploy gate NOTRUN.** Seen on orcd-mini (`784bcc6ee`, two
`tiny_files.py` writers, ~16 M files) after a 3 s `perf --call-graph dwarf`
capture stalled the group-2 leader n2 at 12:54:41–44Z
([profile, p4](../status/orcd-mini-profile-08cc16af4-20261022.md)).

**What happened.** The sequence is reconstructed from the three nodes'
`raft.log` files: a read-only record scan of each group's ENTRY, TRUNC,
HARD, SNAP and CFG records.
1. n2, as term-62 leader, appended entries 30,929,219–30,929,230 in term 62.
   They reached neither n1 nor n3.
2. n1 and n3 ended term 62 at 30,929,218. n1 won term 63 and wrote its
   no-op at 30,929,219 in term 63; n3 holds the same.
3. n2 stepped down to term 63. n1 then sent it an InstallSnapshot of n1's
   12:41 snapshot (index 30,676,477; n2 logged `CFG` and
   `SNAP last=30676477/54`).
4. n2 had already applied past that index, so it took the
   "already applied" branch, `snap_installed(…, take_cfg=0)`. That branch
   ends with `commit_index = min(leader_commit, last_i)`, where `last_i` is
   the **follower's own** log tail. n2's tail still held its unreplicated
   term-62 entries. n2 committed and applied 30,929,219@62 at 12:54:49Z,
   three seconds after n1 and n3 had committed 30,929,219@63.
5. The leader walked n2's tail back one truncation per round trip
   (`TRUNC from=30929230` … `30929220`). At 30,929,219 the conflict sat
   at n2's commit index. `on_ae_req` returns `EFS_ERR_PROTO` with no reply
   there, and the pump discards that result, so the walk-back stopped.

   From then on n1 resent the same window every heartbeat. With W145's
   diagnostics deployed, n2 showed `proto_drops` rising by about 20/s
   (`AE conflict at index=30929219 <= commit=30929219 … refused without
   reply`), and n1 showed `next=30929220`, `match=0` and
   `reject_hint=30929219` for peer 1.

**Consequences.**
- n2's group-2 state machine applied an entry the cluster never committed.
- Reads routed to n2 wait (`read-sleep`/`apply-sleep` at 400 ms).
- Open check: the entry (command tag 1) was proposed at n2. If n2's waiting
  proposer saw it applied with a matching term, a client may have been told
  that an operation succeeded which the cluster never committed.

**Fix (source).**
- `snap_installed` may advance `commit_index` only to
  `min(leader_commit, incl)`. The snapshot proves its own last index and
  nothing after it, and a matching AppendEntries proves the tail.
- `tests/test_raft.c` `test_snapshot_commit_stops_at_snapshot` replays
  n2's case. It FAILs on the old code: the stale tail commits and applies,
  and the leader's replacement cannot land. It PASSes with the fix.

**Diagnostics added** (`22a2207cd`, plus election and step-down lines):
- `raft-status` shows each group's last log index and term, snapshot index,
  rejects sent and protocol drops. On the leader it shows each peer's
  next/match index, in-flight batch and age, ACK age, batches
  sent/refused/blocked/failed, and rejects with their hint.
- Follower refusals log every 10 s; silent `PROTO` refusals always log;
  oversize inbox frames are counted.
- Elections, votes, step-downs (with the commit quorum and match table)
  and any commit by a non-leader are logged.
- `scripts/w145_deposed_leader.sh` reproduces deposition on a private
  cluster; its SIGSTOP and perf modes passed without reproducing.

**Deployed** `76614e8e8` on orcd-mini (2026-10-22 14:22Z):
- `make test` 816/816 with one environmental failure; POSIX smoke 216/216;
  3/3 identical versions.
- The first swap left n3 on the old build: `stop.sh` did not stop it, and
  `start.sh` then refused n2. The cluster was down about 14:20–14:22Z until
  a second clean stop and start. The swap script now refuses to switch
  until every efsd has exited.
- Startup elections moved group 2 from term 149 to 291. The cause is not
  yet examined.
- As expected, n2 is still wedged: its committed 30,929,219@62 is on disk,
  and `proto_drops` keeps rising. The fix prevents new cases; it does not
  repair n2.

**n2 repair (2026-10-22, with the user's go-ahead).**
- No existing path could make a leader send n2 a snapshot, so
  `613bb2c78` added the operator-only `efs-mgmt raft-resync`.
- The first attempts exposed two more bugs:
  - [W146](#w146): images over 4 GiB could not be imported;
  - [W147](#w147): a transfer restarted on every send while the leader
    committed.

  Both were fixed (`e75391268`, `a569de971`).
- On `a569de971`, `raft-resync 10.1.99.1:17433 2` (16:15:59Z) led n3 to send
  its 5.2 GB image. n2 imported it as a full diff (3,769,881 keys) and
  installed it at index 33,953,093 (16:20:33Z), replacing its stray
  30,929,219@62.
- Afterwards all three nodes were at group-2 commit and applied 33,967,666,
  the request had cleared, n2 logged no `read-sleep`/`apply-sleep`, and
  POSIX smoke was 216/216.
- Each deploy restart took about 3 minutes, because n2's shutdown waited for
  a handler stuck in a group-2 read and `stop.sh` gave up on the remaining
  daemon. The guarded swap script retried.

**Remaining.**
1. Find why the new leader sent a 4.7 GB snapshot to a follower that was
   only a few entries behind, instead of walking its tail back.
   - Likely cause: any rejection with `match_index` 0 (for example a
     stale-term reply) resets the leader's `next_index` to 1, below its
     log floor.
2. Check whether a client was acknowledged for index 30,929,219@62.
3. Every restart today ran hundreds of elections: group 2 went from term
   511 to 721 to 923 to 1121.
4. A daemon blocked in a group read delays its shutdown past `stop.sh`'s
   wait. `stop.sh` then leaves the remaining daemons running.

**K1 follow-up (branch `devel-k01`,
[status note](../status/k01-w145-remaining-20261022.md)).**
1. Snapshot to a near follower: fixed in `48d14a37d`. The new leader's
   first commit/read probe went out with `prev_index` 0; its success reply
   (match 0) set `next_index` to 1, below the log floor. A success now never
   lowers `next_index`, and a prev-term conflict hints below the whole
   uncommitted run of the conflicting term. Unit tests FAIL on the old code
   and PASS with the fix.
2. Acknowledged write: **not acknowledged.** All 26 n2 waits on
   30,929,219–30,929,230 ended at the 400 ms deadline with
   `applied=30929217/30929218` (12:54:45.943–46.986Z), so their handlers
   returned BUSY. n2 applied the stray 30,929,219@62 at 12:54:49Z, over two
   seconds later. A verdict needs `applied >= idx` inside one bounded wait
   and a matching term; no caller re-waits on the same (index, term). The
   clients logged only successful retries. n2's raft.log no longer holds
   the record (replaced by the 16:20Z resync); the efsd and fuse logs still
   cover the window.
3. Restart election storms: fixed in `dd876e069` with pre-vote. A node
   campaigned alone from the moment its groups started until its peers
   listened (n3: term 923 -> 1120 in 33 s, then deposed the leader). The
   vote/election/step-down lines are rate limited per group. Unit tests
   FAIL on the old code and PASS; on a private efs1 cluster a staggered
   restart moved terms 1 -> 20/18 before and 1 -> 2 after.
4. Blocked handler at stop: fixed in `781df5750`. A pooled RDMA client
   kept one handler serving retried group reads (no quorum while peers
   stopped); TCP `SHUT_RD` does not reach the RDMA channel. Handlers now
   close before the next request once a stop begins, and the drain is
   bounded at 40 s (refuse, log, exit rc 3 without teardown). Unit test
   PASS; the RDMA case was not reproduced on a cluster.

**Gates.**
- `make test` PASS (done).
- orcd-mini deploy, with n2 back in sync after its repair (done, 16:20Z).
- A private reproduction of deposed leader + snapshot under load, with the
  deposed leader catching up and no stale commit.

<a id="w146"></a>
### W146 — A snapshot image over 4 GiB can never be installed

**Correctness/liveness; opened and closed 2026-10-22.** Deployed in `e75391268`. Gate PASS: n2 installed the 5.2 GB group-2 image on orcd-mini (16:20Z; import diff of 3,769,881 keys).
Found while repairing W145 on orcd-mini. The group-2 snapshot image is 5.2 GB
(group 0's is 5.4 GB). A follower installing it reads both the incoming and
its local image whole through `read_whole`, which refused any file over
`0xffffffff` bytes with `EFS_ERR_NOMEM`. Every install failed after the
transfer (`raft-snap: import diff group=2 rc=-2 n=0`), and the leader
re-exported and re-sent the 5.2 GB image about every 45 s. Any follower
that falls below a leader's log floor at this scale could never catch up.

**Fix.** `read_whole`, `parse_image` and `efs_kv_group_import_prepare` use
64-bit image lengths and offsets. The image format is unchanged: a 32-bit
entry count and 32-bit key and value lengths. The import still holds both
images in memory, about 10 GB for group 2 on orcd-mini.
`test_kv_lsm`, `test_kv_snapshot_tail`, `test_raft_store` and `test_raft`
PASS. `make test` 816/816 with one environmental failure. A unit test with
an image over 4 GiB is too heavy for the suite; the gate is a live install.

**Gate.** An InstallSnapshot of an image over 4 GiB completes on orcd-mini
(the W145 n2 repair).

<a id="w147"></a>
### W147 — A snapshot transfer restarts on every send while the leader commits

**Liveness; opened and closed 2026-10-22.** Deployed in `a569de971`. Gate PASS: n2's group-2 transfer completed on orcd-mini while the group committed, with no re-export. Found while
repairing W145 on orcd-mini.
- The group-2 leader's stored snapshot point (30,676,475) had no file. Its
  `snap-2-*.kvx` had been rotated away; a restart keeps only the index.
- In that case `send_snap` re-exported at the **current** applied index on
  every call. The group kept committing, so each export got a new index, the
  peer's transfer offset reset to 0, and a new 5.2 GB image was exported
  about every 45 s.
- n2's partial file stalled at 46 MB. Any follower needing a snapshot at
  this scale would see the same, as long as the group commits during a
  transfer.

**Fix.** When the stored snapshot point has no file and a newer image is
already open whose index is still in the log, `send_snap` keeps sending that
image. It re-exports only when no usable image is open.

While a W145 resync is requested, the follower's "prev beyond log" rejection
also carries `match_index` 0. Its untrusted tail must not pull the leader
out of the transfer and back into the conflicting AppendEntries.

`tests/test_raft.c` `test_snap_transfer_survives_commits`: a restarted leader
whose snapshot file is gone transfers a multi-chunk image while committing
between chunks.
- On the old code: FAIL (the transfer never completes; one export per send).
- With the fix: PASS (the transfer completes with at most two exports).

**Gate.** n2's group-2 InstallSnapshot completes on orcd-mini (the W145
repair, together with W146).

<a id="w150"></a>
### W150 — No test for the abandon scan's work-budget stop and resume

**Test coverage; opened 2026-10-22 from the [packing validate-once review](../status/review-pack-validate-once-20261022.md); FIXED on `devel-k25` (October 22).**
- `efs_pack_abandon_scan` (`src/meta/pack_mapping.c`) is bounded by
  `efs_kv_lsm_scan_work`, which counts tombstones. A stop by that budget
  resumes after the work cursor, not the callback's last live key.
- `tests/test_pack_validate_once.c` drove only callback stops on the memory
  store, so the work-cursor path, a tombstone-only window and the term
  restart had no test.

**Fix (test only, no change to the scan).** `abandon_sweep_work_bound` runs
on an LSM store with 48 objects of four owner/state kinds, interleaved with
0–16 flushed-then-deleted generations each, before the first object and
after the last. Each bounded call checks that the budget counts tombstones
and that the cursor strictly advances or wraps. The test also covers:
- one pass finds every actionable object exactly once; the first window
  holds tombstones only, and the budget stops most windows;
- wraparound: the next pass finds the same set again;
- mutation mid-pass: an object ahead is cancelled and a new one admitted,
  and the pass reports exactly the current set;
- term change: continuing the old cursor misses this node's earlier
  admissions, and the packer's restart finds them all in one pass;
- budget edges: a budget equal to the measured key count wraps in one call;
  one key short stops just before an actionable last key, and the next
  window reports it and wraps.

**Check that it catches defects (efs3, then reverted).** A scan that drops
the work cursor fails the new case at the cursor-advance check. That
mutation passes the old memory-store cases. An inclusive resume fails
both. Gate: `make test` on efs3, in the K25 report.

**Raw evidence note (2026-10-23):** the bulk data in `gc-buffered-3ohdte4d` (copied stores, generated payloads and build trees) was deleted. Text logs, results and profiler captures remain under `/data1/efs/evidence/`, each with a `PRUNED.txt` listing what was removed. Reproduce the bulk with the method on this page.


## Appendix 6 — Naming

*Source: `how-it-works/naming.md` (headers demoted, nav stripped, links rebased to `docs/how-it-works/`).* **Authority: normative protocol.**

**Naming intent.** The bar for this design is that it earns the *idea* of an
"extreme filesystem": it scales as close as possible to the raw hardware.
Every design decision is checked against that bar — a component is wrong if
it serializes work the hardware could have done in parallel.

**On the name itself.** "extremfs" is close in spelling and sound to the
existing [XtreemFS project](https://www.xtreemfs.org/), whose site attributes
its trademark registration to Quobyte. "EFS" is also the name used for
[Amazon Elastic File System](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/).
These primary-source identity checks were made Oct 7, 2026; they do not
establish trademark clearance or quantify search-engine dominance.

A distinctive, searchable public name remains a design goal, deliberately
open pending a proper name/search check. This project continues to use "efs"
as its working name; this review does not choose or approve a replacement.
Earlier wording is [preserved](../archive/naming-wording-before-round5-20261007.md).


## Appendix 7 — Design rationale

*Source: `how-it-works/design-rationale.md` (headers demoted, nav stripped, links rebased to `docs/how-it-works/`).* **Authority: rationale (explains the index; never overrides it).**

This is the rationale document: why the architecture in
[architecture.md](#architecture) has the shape it has, what is
claimed and what is not, and what was deliberately rejected. The spec itself
is normative; this file argues for it. Accepted design reasoning is not an
implementation or release certificate; the [public-path matrix](../status/spec-implementation.md)
and named acceptance records define the current limits.

Let's be precise about what is and isn't claimed. **Raft-per-shard over an
embedded KV is not a new mechanism.** The claim is stronger than novelty: the
design is a *consequence of the constraints*, and the argument is a
derivation, not an analogy. A copy-cat cites a working system and imitates
it. A derivation starts from what must be true and shows which shapes
survive.

### The constraints are forces, not preferences

| Constraint | Force it exerts | Design it eliminates |
|---|---|---|
| 2³² objects on 4 nodes | ~512 GiB+ of metadata cannot live in RAM | the former fully-in-RAM table |
| immediate cross-client visibility | no authoritative cache may go stale | TTL / negative / attr caches as truth |
| survive f nodes down, read *and* write | a write must commit without the dead nodes | single-coordinator 2PC, primary-backup without failover |
| 3 → 64 nodes | work must spread, not funnel to one writer | a single cluster-wide metadata primary |
| **scale with raw hardware** | parallel work must not hit a software serializer | whole-table flush; per-write inode-row mutation |

### The constraints strongly favor one family; efs picks proven primitives within it

The constraints do not *mathematically* force "Raft + ordered KV"
specifically — Multi-Paxos or Viewstamped Replication, and a B-tree or LSM or
custom page store, satisfy the same forces. The honest statement:

> The constraints strongly favor a **partitioned replicated state machine
> with persistent, paged applied state**. efs chooses **Raft** and an
> **ordered embedded KV** because they satisfy those requirements with
> proven, understandable primitives and minimal new protocol invention.

That this is also where Ceph and CockroachDB landed is not imitation — it is
convergent evolution. The same forces act on any strongly-consistent,
horizontally-scaled, fault-tolerant store, so independent systems solve the
same equations and arrive at the same shape. Convergence is evidence the
derivation is correct, not that it was copied.

### The safety properties are inherited theorems plus explicit composition obligations

- **Core shard-replication safety is inherited from Raft** when implemented
  according to its assumptions (election restriction, log matching, commit
  rules, safe reconfiguration). Leader completeness (I2) is Raft's theorem,
  not majority intersection alone.
**D36 overrides the earlier node-count ladder.** Three nodes are minimum; four
provide the maximum two-loss safety target; larger clusters add scale. Majority
Raft alone cannot meet the four-node requirement. Its replacement/composition
proof remains open; never weaken the target to match current implementation.

- **Quorum durability** (I10/I11): a majority-acknowledged write survives any
  failure that leaves a majority. With RF = 2f+1 that tolerates f losses within the
  Raft failure envelope, provided the durable-ACK and storage assumptions are
  actually satisfied. The production fragment barrier remains [W71](#w71);
  Raft quorum math alone does not certify those writes.
- **EFS-specific composition is *not* covered by Raft's proof.** RPC dedup,
  KV persistence ordering, cross-shard transaction logic, FUSE cache
  coherence, EC generation publication, chunk RMW, reconfiguration, and the
  orphan lifecycle remain **explicit proof / model / simulation
  obligations**. That is exactly what the
  [simulator](#appendix-15--verification--simulator--codesignal-cycle) is for.

### What is genuinely ours — stated precisely

Let us be exact about the claim, because overclaiming here would be both
wrong and unsupportable. **Every primitive in this design has existed:**
Raft, distributed metadata, RDMA, erasure coding, immutable generations,
ordered KV stores, directory sharding, deterministic simulation. Several
systems illustrate individual parts. Primary-source pointers checked Oct 7,
2026 provide context, not an exhaustive prior-art search or comparative ranking:

- [WEKA's current cluster overview](https://docs.weka.io/weka-system-overview/weka-containers-architecture-overview.md)
  describes drive, compute, frontend and management processes distributed
  across server containers. That description does not by itself prove every
  earlier claim about hash placement or complete POSIX semantics.
- [DAOS DFS/dfuse documentation](https://docs.daos.io/master/user/filesystem/)
  describes its POSIX namespace/API and currently lists hard links and flock
  among limitations. This is a versioned interface statement, not a claim that
  EFS already implements all those semantics or that future DAOS releases cannot.
- [VAST's architecture white paper](https://www.vastdata.com/whitepaper)
  describes disaggregated shared-everything storage and shared metadata/
  transaction state; it is a different architectural composition.
- [CephFS metadata documentation](https://docs.ceph.com/en/latest/cephfs/mdcache/)
  distinguishes client-direct RADOS data access from MDS-managed inode and
  directory metadata. An MDS role need not imply dedicated physical hardware.
- [GIGA+](https://www.pdl.cmu.edu/PDSI/gigaplus/index.html) and the
  [IndexFS paper](https://www.pdl.cmu.edu/PDL-FTP/FS/IndexFS-SC14.pdf)
  precede this design's incremental large-directory spreading.
- [FoundationDB's testing documentation](https://apple.github.io/foundationdb/testing.html)
  describes deterministic cluster simulation alongside live and hardware tests.
  Simulation alone is not physical fault acceptance.

Earlier unsourced comparison wording is [preserved](../archive/comparison-wording-before-round5-20261007.md).
We are not claiming to have invented these mechanisms.

**The claim is the composition and the governing principle.** What we have
sought is this combination as one open POSIX filesystem; the following is a
design goal, not proof that no existing public system has the same composition:

```text
POSIX namespace
  + no dedicated MDS tier
  + metadata authority distributed across ordinary storage nodes
  + Raft only for small authoritative metadata state
  + client-direct RDMA data path
  + k+f EC immutable chunk generations
  + no whole-file serialization for parallel writers
  + no inode serialization where independent chunks can proceed
  + directory locality until it becomes a bottleneck
  + failure correctness designed before performance tuning
  + deterministic protocol simulation
  + small-cluster simplicity
```

And the principles that tie it together — the things that, if we execute
them, are the actual contribution
([§0 of the spec](#architecture)):

> **P1 · Never serialize work that the semantics and the hardware allow to
> happen in parallel.**
> **P2 · Co-locate what must commit atomically on the common path; distribute
> what can evolve independently.**
> **P3 · Make stale work harmless instead of trying to prevent it.**

Traditional PFS architectures handle `1000 clients → 1000 different files`
well. The hard problem is `1000 clients → ONE file → different byte/chunk
ranges`. efs's answer is that if writes do not conflict, the filesystem must
