  ```text
                  commits the same zero hole on its behalf
  ```

  **Retirement after a lost reply is decided once (K15/W64).** A reserve
  whose reply never arrives leaves a committed OPEN reservation that its
  owner cannot complete, because the owner never learned the offset. Only
  two facts authorize retiring it; a timer is not one of them, because a
  live owner that did receive the reply may still be writing:

  ```text
  owner fenced     global revocation done and the shard's local rejection
                   floor is above the epoch -> cleanup-appends resolves its
                   OPEN rows as FENCED_HOLE (session cleanup)
  owner abandons   the live owner gives up on the write and sends an
                   abandon for that exact identity (uuid, epoch, seq, len)
                   under its established session -> the receipt result
                   becomes STALE and an OPEN row resolves as ABORTED_HOLE
  ```

  Both run as one exact-image transaction over the owner's session row,
  inode, receipt, reservation, cursor and lane barriers. The resolved row
  records its outcome (completed, aborted hole or fenced hole). The first
  resolution in the log wins. A retirement over a completed row is a no-op.
  A completion over a hole-retired row is refused STALE and never applied.
  A completion that is decided but not yet resolved holds its intents, so
  a concurrent retirement aborts and retries rather than overtaking it.
  Because the abandon retires the receipt, a delayed reserve or replay of
  that identity is refused STALE and can never allocate or learn the
  offset. A reserve that never applied is therefore never applied later.
  On the wire, the abandon is the ordinary APPEND request with
  `EFS_APPEND_ABANDON` set in `len`. If the abandon cannot be delivered,
  the client still releases the identity, and its later ACK forbids any
  new allocation under it. The stranded row then waits for session fencing
  or the last-close drain, which is the fail-closed backstop.

  The client is *required* to resolve a reservation it cannot complete;
  session fencing is the backstop for a client that stops participating
  altogether, not the ordinary path. Each resolution is a deliberate
  committed state, never an emergent one, and each unblocks the frontier for
  everyone queued behind it. The
  precise POSIX statement: a hole arises only from a write that never
  returned success, it reads as zeros (indistinguishable from a sparse
  region), and no returned write is ever lost. Reservations are never
  rolled back, because later appenders already received offsets past them.

#### W52 serialized completion command — candidate implementation

The NUC candidate completes all reservations covered by an already committed
REPORT EOF in one inode-group `APPEND_CATCHUP` entry. It does not publish chunks
or recompute EOF from a replica's lane view. The host subsequently waits for a
guarded cross-shard transaction to retire lane barriers before replying to
REPORT. A partial publication retains the remaining barriers. Implementation
and outstanding live acceptance are recorded in the
[W52/NUC ledger](../status/nuc-w52-w97-resume-20261011.md).

The internal Raft command uses big-endian integers:

| Byte offset | Field | Bytes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Command tag, 52 | 1 |
| 1 | Inode | 8 |
| 9 | Inode generation | 8 |
| 17 | Content epoch | 8 |
| 25 | Previously published EOF | 8 |
| 33 | Captured outstanding-reservation allocation bound | 4 |
| 37 | Session present, exactly 0 or 1 | 1 |
| 38 | Client UUID, present only when the flag is 1 | 16 |
| 54 | Session epoch, present only when the flag is 1 | 4 |

Exactly 38 or 58 bytes are accepted, on the inode's Raft group only. Generation,
content epoch, session and intent checks precede mutation. Completion rows and
the cursor share one atomic KV apply scope with the applied marker. IO or
allocation failure discards the scope and retries the committed entry; logical
refusals advance the log with a failed verdict. A lost reply after completion
retries barrier retirement without another completion proposal.

The existing scope admits at most 32,766 outstanding reservations and scan rows.
An outstanding count above the captured bound returns BUSY for recapture; an
unsupported backlog returns OVERFLOW before mutation. There is no serial
per-reservation fallback or widened request timeout. All voters must understand
tag 52 before admission. No persistent row format changes, but an old binary
must not replay a log containing an uncheckpointed command it cannot decode.

### Packed small files (W125)

**The write path is unchanged; packing happens after close.** A file of at
most `EFS_PACK_THRESHOLD` (16 KiB) is written and published as per-file
chunk fragments like any file. Its chunk-zero publication also records the
file in its group's **candidate index** (KV kind 46, key epoch + FileID, the
epoch being leader time / 60 s, `EFS_PACK_EPOCH_S`), in the same batch.
The entry's value is the inode generation and a publish stamp (the file's
lane sequence after that publication). `PACK_UNINDEX` (MD 77) carries the
value the packer read and deletes an entry only on an exact match, so a
rewrite (an `O_TRUNC` that the packer saw at size 0, then new bytes) whose
publication re-added the entry before the unindex committed stays a
candidate.

**Packer (group leader).** For each led group the packer selects
candidates that are closed, quiet for the minimum age (60 s), linked,
single-chunk and not leased; groups them by (epoch, parent directory,
inode); reads their bytes (data fragment 0 of base and spans, or fragments
1 and 2 XORed); builds a segment (`packed_segment` v2: 96 B header, 72 B
per record, at most 512 records, records up to 16 KiB, per-record digests)
and encodes it 2+1.

**Admission, upload, switch:**
1. `PACK_ADMIT` (MD 73) stores the segment object (KV kind 45: ledger v2
   plus placement) with every record PENDING, before any fragment exists,
   and makes the store require reader capability PACK_V2 (older builds
   refuse the store).
   Placement is three distinct live members of the data ring keyed by the
   segment id (`efs_pack_destinations`), not the group's voters (D38): a
   segment may live entirely on nodes that host no metadata group.
2. `PUT_SEGMENT` (wire 157) writes each fragment to its node, which checks
   by a linearizable read that the object is admitted, ACTIVE and places
   this exact fragment there, and fsyncs file and directory before replying.
   A node that hosts the group reads after its own ReadIndex; any other node
   asks a voter with `PACK_OBJECT_READ` (wire 173/174: routed leader first,
   then each voter; the voter answers only if it hosts the group, after its
   ReadIndex). Any transport error, refusal or bad reply refuses the PUT;
   segment reclaim uses the same read and stays BUSY on failure.
3. `PACK_SWITCH` (MD 74) moves up to 128 files in one entry. Each member's
   source is the digest of its stored chunk-zero row; it switches only if
   the inode generation matches, the file is linked and unleased, the row
   still hashes to that digest, and the new reference carries the row's
   newest content epoch and a fresh record generation. Switched records
   become LIVE; the superseded per-file generation and spans become GC
   records; a replaced packed record is released. Other members are
   CANCELLED (dead bytes).
4. `PACK_CANCEL` (MD 75) abandons remaining PENDING records (failed copy,
   deposed packer).

A copy with two fragments acknowledged and the third not (a member down
before the heartbeat says so, or refusing) switches only after
`PACK_DEGRADED` MARK for that fragment has committed and the leader's
replica holds it; with fewer than two, or no mark, the copy is cancelled.
Compaction writes its output segments the same way.

**Segment rebuild on return (K37).** `PACK_DEGRADED` (MD 247:
`[group][op][id:8][generation:8][mask][reason]`) keeps one row per segment
(KV kind 249 on the group's anchor shard, value `[mask][reasons][0:2]`):
MARK adds mask bits on an ACTIVE segment; CLEAR deletes a one-bit mark
that still names exactly that fragment; RETIRE deletes a mark whose segment
is gone or holds no live or pending record; `PACK_RETIRE` deletes the mark
with the segment. Each group leader, in its GC loop:
- **Audit:** probes each available member with `SEGMENT_AUDIT` (wire
  241/242) at most every 2 s; a member reports its incarnation, whether a
  leader of this group completed a sweep of that incarnation, and whether
  its stores are settled (no root recovery-uncertain after an unclean stop).
  An unswept, settled member gets a sweep of the group's published segments
  (no PENDING record) from a cursor, at most 256 fragments per pass; it reads
  and verifies each named file (size, I25 record, recorded digest, payload
  hash) and answers OK, MISSING, BAD or ERROR. MISSING and BAD are marked;
  ERROR leaves the sweep open, to start over after 30 s. Only a sweep with a
  verdict for every fragment is reported complete, and the member records
  it for its incarnation, so a new leader does not repeat it.
- **Rebuild:** marks are walked from a cursor (at most 64 rebuilds and 1 s
  per pass). A segment no longer live is retired; a mark with two bits is
  reported unrecoverable and kept; otherwise, once all three placement
  nodes are available, the two present fragments are read and checked
  against the segment checksums, the third is rebuilt by XOR and checked,
  stored with `PUT_SEGMENT` flag `EFS_SEGMENT_PUT_F_REBUILD` (the storage
  node accepts it only while `PACK_OBJECT_READ` returns that exact one-bit
  mask beside the object, replaces a torn or foreign copy and fsyncs before
  replying), audited on that node, and only then cleared. A source fragment
  its holder proves MISSING or BAD adds its bit: the segment is reported
  unrecoverable and its files read EIO until rewritten or removed.
`efs-mgmt status` prints `Degraded segments: N (group 0: a, group 2: b);
unrecoverable=U ...`; the cluster state is DEGRADED while N > 0, and
`Protection:` reads LOST while U > 0.

**Ledger and reclaim.** Every path that drops or replaces a packed row
(overwrite, truncate, lane sweep, reap) releases its record in the same
batch, so live/dead bytes always match the mappings. A segment with no
live or pending record is RECLAIMING; the retirement pass hands it to every
member's reclaim journal (`GC_SEGMENT_BATCH`, wire 161; journal record kind
SEGMENT, fenced, deleted later) and `PACK_RETIRE` (MD 76) forgets it.
Superseded per-file fragments go to the journals in batches
(`GC_FRAG_BATCH`, wire 163; kind SUPERSEDED, checksum-guarded deletion
and removal of empty chunk and inode directories).

**Budget.** Packing runs at the idle rate (5,000 files/s per group) unless
the group is busy, meaning foreground commits exceed 100/s, measured over
windows of at least 1 s. While busy, it drops to a floor of 50 files/s and
ramps back towards the idle rate only under space pressure. Pressure is the
larger of two linear ramps:

- unpacked candidate bytes, estimated as backlog × 64 KiB, from 64 GiB to
  128 GiB;
- the highest member quota usage, from 50% to 80%.

The busy rate is `floor + (idle − floor) × pressure`. The backlog is
counted every 30 s. A pass reads its segments' files on 16 threads and
builds and switches its segments concurrently (`EFS_PACK_SEGMENTS_PER_PASS`, at most 32). Passes run back to
back while backlog and budget remain.

**Segment quota reserve.** `PUT_SEGMENT` may exceed a node's quota by
quota/64, clamped to 16–256 MiB. Packing frees more than it writes, since
each file's 69,632-byte fragments shrink to a share of a segment. Without
the reserve, a node at quota could never pack its way back under it.

**Compaction.** Compaction is scheduled maintenance, separate from packing
passes and from foreground I/O. It considers every ACTIVE segment that has
a hole, and underfilled segments (under 8 KiB live), which are merged
together. The whole segment index is scanned and the 64 highest-priority
candidates are kept. Priority is `0.5 × live fraction + 0.5 × coldness`:

- the live-fraction term clears tiny holes first;
- coldness is age over 24 h, capped at 1; compacted output counts as cold.

So a cluster left idle or read-only long enough ends with no holes. Live
records are read back and switched into cold segments, the same way
packing switches files. Compaction runs on three triggers:

- **Idle:** after 60 s without busy load, a batch of up to 256 output
  segments, capped at 10 s of work per batch, repeated every 60 s while
  idle. Reads are not commits, so a read-only cluster counts as idle.
- **Daily:** a UTC window (default 03:00 for 120 min) runs
  `segments_per_pass` per pass whenever the group is not busy.
- **Operator:** `efs-mgmt pack-compact <node:port> [segments]` (wire
  167/168) queues a request on every group the node leads and runs even
  while busy. With `0` it only prints the fragmentation summary.

Each leader logs a `packer: segments` fragmentation summary every 30 s:
segments, live, dead, holed, underfilled and compacted total.

**Backfill.** `PACK_INDEX` (MD 78) backfills the candidate index from a
leader scan of inode shards, for stores written before packing.

**Tunables** (efsd environment; defaults in parentheses):

| Variable | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `EFS_PACK_MIN_AGE_MS` (60000) | quiet time before a closed file is packed |
| `EFS_PACK_FILES_PER_S` (5000) | idle packing rate per group |
| `EFS_PACK_BUSY_FILES_PER_S` (50) | floor while busy |
| `EFS_PACK_BUSY_COMMITS_PER_S` (100) | foreground commit rate that counts as busy |
| `EFS_PACK_UNPACKED_GIB` (64) | unpacked bytes where pressure starts (full at 2×) |
| `EFS_PACK_SPACE_START_PCT` / `_FULL_PCT` (50 / 80) | quota-usage pressure ramp |
| `EFS_PACK_SEGMENTS_PER_PASS` (8) | segments per pass, and compaction per daily pass |
| `EFS_PACK_COMPACT_IDLE_S` (60) | idle time before idle compaction |
| `EFS_PACK_COMPACT_IDLE_SEGS` (256) | output segments per idle batch |
| `EFS_PACK_COMPACT_DAILY_START_MIN` (180) | daily window start, UTC minute of day |
| `EFS_PACK_BACKFILL_SHARDS` (64) | inode shards scanned per backfill step |

Built in since A6 (a set variable stops efsd): a 10 s work cap per idle
compaction batch, a 120 min daily window and full coldness at 86400 s
([inventory](../status/a6-settings-inventory-20261024.md)).

**Reads.** GETCHUNKS returns a packed base with `EFS_CHUNK_REC_F_PACKED`
and the 96-byte reference; nodes and checksums are the segment's. The
client fetches any two segment fragments with `GET_SEGMENT` (wire 159),
hashes each, decodes, checks the record against the reference, zero-fills
past it and overlays spans. The scratch buffers come from the demand-read
allowance (below). Connections must first declare protocol 2
(`CLIENT_HELLO`, wire 165); the server answers GETCHUNKS and segment
messages only on declared connections, and a new client refuses to mount
daemons that do not accept the declaration.

**Read headroom.** Demand reads, including packed-segment scratch, may use
the client buffer pool's hard and drain budgets plus a read allowance
(`EFS_DCACHE_READ_BYTES`, 64 MiB). Dirty write data cannot hold that
allowance, so a heavy writer can no longer starve readers into
ENOMEM/EBUSY. A read that cannot get buffers waits until its deadline
(30 s when it has none) instead of failing at once.

**Modification.** Writes, appends and truncates of a packed file use the
ordinary write path: a full rewrite releases the record; spans over a
packed base are read together with it and re-index the file, which the
packer then repacks; a write that takes the file past the packing
threshold is never a span: the client folds chunk zero (packed base plus
the new bytes) into an ordinary per-file base, whose publication releases
the record, so no file above the threshold keeps a packed base under
spans; a truncate keeps a packed tail like a span chain (the size and
epoch fence hide bytes past EOF; extended by truncate, the file reads
zeros past the record). Hole punch is not supported for any file.

### Stale-target fencing — targets are dumb, metadata decides

Because clients write directly to data targets, Raft terms on the metadata
path do not fence the data path. But the fencing is *not* "target rejects an
older generation" — generations are immutable candidate objects, and two
concurrent clients may legitimately produce different candidate generations
for the same chunk with no global ordering between them. The correct model:

- A fragment object `(FileID, chunk_index, candidate_generation,
  fragment_index, coding_profile_id)` is **immutable and its PUT is
  idempotent**. A target stores it; storing the same object twice is a
  no-op. A target may hold several candidate generations of one chunk at
  once — that is fine, because they are distinct immutable objects.
- The target verifies only **placement epoch, target incarnation, and object
  identity** — i.e. "am I the current, legitimate home for this object?" It
  does **not** decide which candidate generation is logically newer, and it
  does **not** check client sessions (a fenced client's PUT just stores an
  orphan; publication is rejected on the metadata path — see
  [sessions.md](#appendix-12--protocol--sessions-open-unlinked-locking)).
- **The metadata authority alone decides which generation is committed**
  (via the publication CAS). Unpublished candidates are orphans, reclaimed
  without touching committed state (I15).

This keeps the data nodes dumb — which fits the minimalist design — and it is
what makes I20 precise: a stale writer cannot make its generation *visible*,
because visibility is granted only by the metadata publication protocol, not
by anything a data target does.

#### Publication validates the durability evidence

Dumb targets have a consequence that must be stated, or the model has a hole:
if nobody on the data path checks the coding and placement contract, then
**the metadata publication authority is the only place it can be checked**,
and it must actually do so. A stale client can hold an old placement view and
successfully write a full, durable stripe *to the wrong set of targets*.
Those PUTs are harmless in themselves (P3) — but the publication naming them
must be rejected, not accepted because "k+f ACKs arrived."

A publication therefore carries its evidence, and the lane leader validates
it before the entry is committed:

```text
publication = { FileID, content_epoch, chunk_index,
                candidate_generation,
                coding_profile_id, placement_epoch,
                durable_ack_set = [ { target incarnation,
                                      fragment role/index,
                                      object identity,
                                      fragment checksum } ... ] }

accept only if:
    coding_profile_id  == the file's current profile
    placement_epoch    == the current placement for those fragments
    the ack set covers exactly the k+f expected fragment roles
    those targets sit in the required number of distinct failure domains
    every ACK names THIS candidate object, not some other generation
    (degraded publication: the relaxed k+(f-u) rule above, and only then)
```

This is what lets targets stay dumb without weakening I11 or I14: the
contract is enforced once, by the authority that decides visibility, instead
of by every target on the fastest path.

#### End-to-end integrity (I25)

The failure model excludes Byzantine *participants*, but silent media
corruption is not Byzantine behavior — it is ordinary SSD/DRAM/wire reality,
and erasure coding is specifically bad at it: EC can reconstruct from a
corrupt fragment and produce confidently wrong data, because the code has no
way to tell which input lied.

So every durable fragment carries a checksum over **its immutable identity
plus its payload** (identity included, so a correct fragment stored under the
wrong name cannot pass). The checksum is verified on read and before any use
as reconstruction input. A fragment that fails verification is treated as
**unavailable** — it is never fed to the decoder, the read is served by
reconstructing from other fragments, and the bad fragment is queued for
repair like any lost one. The immutable-generation design makes this cheap:
the checksum is computed once, at creation, and never has to be maintained.

This also gives the simulator ([verification.md](#appendix-15--verification--simulator--codesignal-cycle)) a
natural corruption fault to inject, which is the only way the property is
ever actually tested.

##### Fragment record format 2 (implemented, W75)

Every fragment file a storage node writes, chunk fragments and packed-segment
fragments alike, is the payload followed by one fixed 128-byte **fragment
record** (`include/efs/frag_record.h`). Buffered roots append the record
directly after the payload. O_DIRECT roots append a 4 KiB tail page that
begins with the record and is zero-padded. There is no sidecar file. All
integers are big-endian.

```text
off  size  field
  0     8  magic "EFSFRAG\0"
  8     2  version = 2
 10     2  kind: 1 chunk fragment, 2 packed-segment fragment
 12     4  record bytes = 128
 16     4  space: export id (chunk) | publication group (segment)
 20     4  fragment index (0 = D1, 1 = D2, 2 = P)
 24     8  object: inode number (chunk) | segment id (segment)
 32     8  generation: chunk candidate generation | segment generation
 40     4  chunk index (0 for a segment)
 44     4  payload length
 48     4  coding profile = 1 (fixed 2+1)
 52     4  reserved, zero
 56    32  payload digest = BLAKE3(payload)
 88    32  bound digest   = BLAKE3(record bytes [0, 88))
120     8  reserved, zero
```

The bound digest covers the identity fields and the payload digest, so it is
a checksum over the immutable identity plus the payload, as I25 requires.
The payload digest is the value that travels on the wire and sits in the
chunk map, so clients, metadata and GC records are unchanged.

**Write.** The PUT handler and the ticketed upload rehash the received
payload before storage, as before. The store then builds the record from
the identity the request names and writes payload and record in one write.
An incomplete identity, such as generation 0, is refused, so no file is
ever written without a record.

**Read.** A GET names export, inode, chunk index, fragment index and
candidate generation. The storage node checks, in order:

1. The record is present and complete. A torn or missing record is
   `EFS_ERR_CHECKSUM`.
2. Magic, version, kind, record size and reserved fields are known. Anything
   else is `EFS_ERR_FRAG_FORMAT`.
3. The bound digest matches. A rotted record is `EFS_ERR_CHECKSUM`.
4. Every identity field equals the requested identity, including the export
   geometry's payload length. A mismatch is `EFS_ERR_FRAG_IDENTITY`.
5. For data fragments, BLAKE3 of the payload equals the payload digest. A
   mismatch is `EFS_ERR_CHECKSUM`. Metadata-table pages stop after step 4,
   because their payload integrity is the EFSR root checksums.

A refused fragment is never served. The node replies with GET status
`EFS_GET_CHUNK_INTEGRITY` and logs `store: I25 get refused fragment <path>:
<reason> field=<name>` (the first 256 refusals, then every 1024th). The
client logs `read: I25 node refused fragment` and treats the fragment as
unavailable. A read then decodes from the other two fragments, which pass the
same server-side checks and are compared with the chunk-map digests captured
by the reader. The node's check ends at its reply buffer, so the client
hashes every received fragment payload (BLAKE3) and compares it with the
reply's digest before the fragment is decoded: TCP checksums and RDMA's ICRC
do not cover host memory or the receive path. There is no switch
([D42 audit](../status/read-verify-audit-20261024.md)). Two refused fragments fail the read with EIO. Nothing is
repaired automatically (W74).

**GC.** The checksum-conditional delete reads the record, verifies identity
and format, and compares the payload digest with the GC record's digest. A
file whose record has an unknown format, another identity or a bad bound
digest is neither deleted nor acknowledged. The GC record stays pending and
the refusal is logged. Whole-inode reclaim of a dead inode removes the
inode's directory without per-file checks, because it removes everything
under that FileID.

**Packed segments.** Segment fragment files use the same record with kind 2.
Segment GET, a retried segment PUT that finds an existing file, and segment
reads all verify the record against `(group, segment id, segment generation,
fragment index, length)` before comparing digests.

**Restart after an unclean stop.** Verified recovery (below) reads every
fragment file whole and proves its record and payload digest; it replaced the
report-only scan of recently modified files.

**Identity fields not in the record.** `content_epoch` is a fence, not
object identity (see above), so it is not bound. The inode generation and
the export salt are not bound either. Neither GET, the GC executor nor the
packer receives them today. Fragment GETs carry only `(export, ino, chunk,
fragment, candidate generation)`, and the client read path does not hold
the inode generation. FileID separation comes from the candidate generation:
it is BLAKE3 of a 128-bit per-process random object UUID, a sequence, and the
chunk index. A fragment of a previous inode incarnation or of an earlier
filesystem therefore carries a different generation and is refused as an
identity mismatch. Binding the inode generation and the salt directly needs
both fields on the GET and GC wire and in the client read path. That is a
separate follow-up.

**No earlier format is read.** The storage root marker (`.efs-engine`) now
records root format 1, meaning fragment record format 2. At startup a root
whose marker names format 0, the payload-only 32-byte digest tail, is
refused, and so is an unmarked root whose `data/` directory is not empty. The error
names the format, for example `storage: <root> has root format 0 (fragment
format 1: payload-only digest tail); this build reads only root format 1
...; refusing startup, reformat the root`. There is no migration. A single
old-format file found inside a format-1 root is refused per file as
`EFS_ERR_FRAG_FORMAT`, or as `EFS_ERR_CHECKSUM` when its 32-byte tail is too
short to hold a record.

#### Verified recovery (K36)

A crash, `SIGKILL`, forced exit (rc 3) or power loss leaves every storage
root of the node "recovery uncertain": PUT acknowledgement is asynchronous,
so fragments acknowledged after the last durable barrier may be missing or
torn. The node fences COMMIT (`fsync` and DATA_COMMIT return `EIO`), across
orderly restarts, until a recovery thread (`src/server/recovery.c`) proves
the store; decision D42, finding F23. A restart, a sampled check or a forced
sync never clears the fence. The phases, each shown in
`efs-mgmt sync-status` and the log:

1. **identity**: every root's durability record names this boot (previous
   boot + 1) as running under this process's verifier; the member store
   advanced the incarnation before anything was served.
2. **journal**: the reclaim journal was verified and replayed at startup, or
   rebuilt by its own recovery thread after a failed verification.
3. **ledgers**: every storage session certificate (the K13 PUT floor) reads
   back intact; `*.tmp.*` leftovers of an interrupted seal are removed.
4. **fragments**: every chunk and segment fragment file is read whole, under
   the lock a PUT of that object holds. Its record must name exactly the
   object its file name names, and BLAKE3 of the payload must equal the
   record's digest. A torn, misnamed or corrupt file is dropped (unlinked,
   directory synced, quota credited). A name that is not a fragment name is
   counted and left alone.
5. **raft**: each metadata group the node hosts answers a ReadIndex from this
   node, which returns only once the local replica applied everything its
   leader had committed. A replica whose apply missed a committed row is
   resynced from the leader's snapshot first (as `raft-resync`).
6. **tickets**: every ADMITTED ticket (K13) placing a fragment here whose
   fragment is not proven here is remembered; it may still be published.
7. **metadata**: every published object (chunk base and live span) placing a
   fragment here is checked against the published digest. The inventory is
   read page by page (`EFS_RECOVERY_SCAN_PAGE` records) from the local KV
   after the ReadIndex, or with `EFS_MSG_RECOVERY_SCAN` (243/244) from a member
   hosting a group this node does not host. A missing or mismatching fragment
   is dropped and its stripe gets a W154 degraded mark through Raft
   (`EFS_MD_CMD_RECOVERY_MARK`, tag 248): the mark is written only while the
   chunk row still references exactly that object; an identical mark is
   left as it is; a mark for another fragment of the same object is never
   overwritten (a second loss the 2+1 code cannot rebuild, counted
   `unrecoverable`). Every ACTIVE packed segment holding switched files that
   places a fragment here is checked the same way; one not proven is dropped
   and counted `segments missing`: its two peers still serve it, and W154 has
   no segment rebuild.
8. **fence**: every root's fence clears and COMMIT works again.

After the fence the thread waits for each remembered ticket to leave
ADMITTED (a published one is marked as in 7) and counts the marked fragments
the group leaders rebuild here (`rebuilt`, `rebuild_waiting`). Nothing a
client was promised depends on that tail: the PUT verifier changed with the
unclean boot, so a fragment the previous boot acknowledged and did not
COMMIT stays lost in its client's `fsync` (K35: proven on the other two with
a degraded mark, or `EIO`), never durable, and a crash before the tail
finishes is caught by the next recovery's inventory.

A transient obstacle (no leader yet, a peer unreachable) is retried and shown
as the reason. A failed verification (an unreadable certificate, a fragment
that cannot be removed, a row that does not decode) leaves the node fenced
with `recovery FAILED` and the reason until a restart verifies it. Every step
is idempotent, so a crash during recovery leaves the record unclean and the
next start recovers again. A single node that never formed a cluster cannot
prove its groups and stays fenced. Full power-loss qualification is a
separate scope decision.


## Appendix 11 — Protocol — directory placement & spreading

*Source: `how-it-works/protocols/directory.md` (headers demoted, nav stripped, links rebased to `docs/how-it-works/`).* **Authority: normative protocol.**

**Implementation limits:** accepted ancestry/all-used-lane predicates exceed
the current eight-record namespace guard bound ([W84](#w84)).
ReadIndex-backed observations also require the fresh-authority gate
[W82](#w82). Protocol requirements below remain binding.

This is the placement decision everything else hangs off. The authoritative
operation→participant matrix derived from these rules is
[§6 of the spec](#architecture); this document is the placement
protocol itself.

### Placement rules

- **The inode row lives on `inode_shard(ino)`** ([§5 of the
  spec](../architecture.md) defines the function; this document never
  restates placement formulas, it explains them).
- **A dentry lives on its parent's shard**
  (`dentry_shard = inode_shard(parent_ino)`), with a **threshold-based
  spread** for huge/hot directories (below).

**Why parent-shard dentries.** It makes the two dominant namespace ops
single-shard: `create`/`unlink` inside a directory touch only
`inode_shard(parent)` for the dentry. readdir is one ordered range scan on
one shard. The cost — a hot directory funnels to one leader — is real but
bounded, and it is the *right* trade because directory locality is the common
case.

**The two-index problem, resolved.** The full mutable inode row is **not**
stored in both indexes. The dentry index stores a **projection**:

```text
(parent_ino, name) -> (ino, generation, type)        // dentry: small, lookup hint
(ino)              -> authoritative inode_row        // inode: single source of truth
```

The dentry value carries only what LOOKUP needs to route and to validate a
handle (`ino`, `generation`, `type`). All mutable attributes (mode, uid, gid,
nlink, …) live **only** in the inode row — with two deliberate exceptions
defined in [the data protocol](#appendix-10--protocol--data-plane): *write-generated* size, mtime and
ctime live in the file's bounded write lanes (otherwise every write would
serialize
on the inode shard), and `stat()` merges them under the double-collect
snapshot protocol. Explicit attribute changes (`utimens`, `chmod`, `chown`,
truncate) always update the inode row. This eliminates any
chmod/chown/mtime/size/nlink divergence between the two indexes, and it makes
hardlinks clean: many `(parent,name)` keys point at one authoritative inode.

**Cost we accept:** a LOOKUP that needs attributes does a dentry get (parent
shard) then an inode get (inode shard) — two point-gets, possibly two shards.
That is the price of not duplicating mutable state, and it is paid only on
the attribute path, not the name-exists path.

### CREATE co-location and directory group affinity

Regular files in LOCAL directories share their parent's numerical shard.
New directories retain a salted numerical shard of their own, while nested
LOCAL directories stay in their parent's metadata Raft group. Root children
continue to distribute independently across both groups.

```text
CREATE regular file:
    normal directory:  inode_shard(new_ino) = inode_shard(parent_ino)
    spread directory:  inode_shard(new_ino) = dentry_shard(parent_ino, name)

MKDIR:
    scattered = hash(parent_ino, name, export_salt) & 0xFFF
    root child:   inode_shard(new_dir) = scattered
    nested child: inode_shard(new_dir) = (scattered & ~1) | (parent_ino & 1)
```

With the current odd/even metadata-group mapping, LOCAL nested MKDIR commits
its parent update, dentry and new inode in one atomic Raft entry even when
those rows occupy different numerical shards. Cross-group and spread-directory
mutations still use [transactions](#appendix-9--protocol--cross-shard-transactions). Recorded CREATE FileIDs
remain authoritative during replay: the exact old scattered choice is accepted
alongside the new selector; unrelated shard hints are rejected. Existing
identities and directories do not move.

This trades group-level distribution within a narrow subtree for fewer durable
transaction waves. Independent top-level projects still distribute across both
groups, and nested directories retain numerical shard spread. Numerical spread
does **not** imply independent current leaders: arbitrary nested projects can
share a group. Hot-directory dentry spreading and file-data placement remain
unchanged. A future group-map expansion must explicitly revisit this policy.

The allocator picks an ino whose low 12 bits equal the required shard (inos
are allocated per-shard — §5 of the spec — so this is free: the shard's
allocator simply hands out its own inos).

**The stranded-set bound still holds, now for files.** A normal directory's
*files* keep their inode rows on the directory's shard forever — their ino
identity encodes the shard (`ino & 0xFFF`) and cannot migrate.
`EFS_DIR_SPREAD_MIN` is therefore a **scalability bound, not just a space
threshold**: it caps how many file rows can be permanently co-located on one
shard before the directory spreads. It is kept low enough that the stranded
set is irrelevant at scale (thousands of rows, never millions).

### Hot-directory spread is a layout-epoch protocol, not a flag

A *normal* directory deliberately serializes its creates on one shard leader
— a locality choice, and the right one (directory locality is the common
case) — which means P1 is satisfied by the *spread mechanism*, not by
pretending the conflict doesn't exist. The spread trigger therefore responds
to **actual serialization pressure, not just namespace size**:

```text
spread when:  entries > EFS_DIR_SPREAD_MIN
           OR sustained op rate / queue depth / latency on the
              directory's shard crosses a pressure threshold
```

The LOCAL inode row carries `nents`, a count of immediate children
(create/mkdir/link dest increment it; unlink/rmdir/a name leaving a directory
decrement it). Crossing `nents > EFS_DIR_SPREAD_MIN` commits `SPLITTING` on
that same parent-row PUT — one Raft entry, no extra round. After spread the
count is frozen; HASHED emptiness is the per-lane `dentry_seq` read set, not
a distributed counter (the spec rejected that). Runtime override:
`EFS_DIR_SPREAD_MIN` (tests). Pressure-triggered spread is specified; the
bound is not a number in the spec and is not invented here. Source review
found size-based admission and migration of already-SPLITTING directories,
but no pressure-based automatic trigger ([W81](#w81)). Draining
SPLITTING leftovers is the background migrator (in-memory queue, GC-thread
pass on the host, opportunistic drain in the sim after a size-trigger
flip). `raft-dir migrate` plus finish stay as the idempotent operator
path.

(a 100-entry directory with 100,000 clients creating and unlinking never
crosses the size threshold but can overload its leader — the required
pressure trigger is intended to catch this case; current size-only admission
does not establish that behavior). Spread is one-way initially: once HASHED, a directory does not
collapse back. And crossing the trigger does not flip a bit — a 100M-entry
directory cannot be re-partitioned atomically, and
lookups/creates/unlinks/readdir must keep working *during* the move. The
directory carries a **layout epoch**:

```text
dir.layout = LOCAL            all dentries on the parent shard
    |
    v  (threshold crossed; owner Raft-commits SPLITTING)
dir.layout = SPLITTING(e)     new writes go to the directory's 64 dentry
                              shards; a migrator moves existing dentries
                              idempotently, in batches
    |
    v  (all dentries moved; owner Raft-commits HASHED)
dir.layout = HASHED(e)        all dentries on the 64 dentry shards; old
                              local range is GC'd
```

Read/write rules during `SPLITTING`: **writes go only to the hashed
location**; **reads check the hashed location first, then the not-yet-moved
local range**; the migrator's moves are idempotent (a dentry already moved is
a no-op), so a crash mid-split resumes cleanly; readdir merges both. The
layout epoch `e` lets a client cache the layout and detect a stale decision.

**Mutations of not-yet-migrated entries use a dominating tombstone** — this
is what enforces I8 (no resurrection) during the split. "Writes go to the
hashed location" is not enough on its own: if `unlink(foo)` only wrote the
hashed side while the old local `foo` still exists, the migrator could later
copy the stale local `foo` into hashed storage and resurrect it. So a
mutation of an entry that has not migrated yet writes an authoritative
hashed record first:

```text
unlink(foo) while foo is still LOCAL-only:
    write HASHED(foo) = TOMBSTONE(layout_epoch = e)

lookup(foo):
    hashed record or tombstone exists  ->  it decides (tombstone => ENOENT);
                                           LOCAL is never consulted
migrator:
    sees TOMBSTONE(epoch >= e) for foo ->  does not copy LOCAL foo
eventually:
    old LOCAL foo is GC'd with the rest of the local range
```

A rename/move out of a not-yet-migrated entry likewise writes the
authoritative hashed overlay record (new name, or tombstone for the old
name) *before* the old local copy is allowed to disappear. Rule: during
`SPLITTING`, **the hashed side always wins over the local side**, for
records and tombstones alike.

### Directory timestamps must spread with the directory

Spreading the dentries is not enough on its own, and this is easy to miss:
POSIX says creating, removing or renaming an entry updates the **containing
directory's** mtime and ctime. If a create that lands on hash shard 77 then
has to bump the directory inode's mtime on shard 12, **every create in the
spread directory still funnels through shard 12** — the spread has been
defeated by a timestamp, and the hot-directory scaling claim is false. This
is precisely the failure mode P1 exists to catch.

The answer is the same shape as file write lanes ([data protocol](#appendix-10--protocol--data-plane)):

```text
LOCAL directory:
    dentry mutation and dir mtime/ctime are on the same shard already
    -> one Raft entry, nothing to do

HASHED directory:
    each dentry shard carries a dir_lane:
        { lane_seq, max_mtime, max_ctime }

    create/unlink/rename on hash shard S:
        { dentry mutation                     <- exclusive key
        ; MAX(dir_lane[S].max_mtime, now)     <- commutative reduction
        ; MAX(dir_lane[S].max_ctime, now) }   <- commutative reduction
        ONE Raft entry on S. The parent shard is not involved.

    stat(directory):
        mtime = MAX( inode.base_mtime, dir_lanes' max_mtime )
        ctime = MAX( inode.base_ctime, dir_lanes' max_ctime )
```

**For that to be bounded, the directory's shard set must be bounded — so a
spread directory uses a fixed 64-shard permutation, exactly like file
lanes.** Hashing names freely over all 4096 shards would let one directory's
used set grow to 4096, and `stat(dir)` with it; "bounded like a file's
lanes" would be wishful. A directory therefore has at most 64 dentry shards,
chosen by the same construction data.md uses for lanes — a name hashes to
one of 64 lanes, and the lane maps to a shard by the odd-stride permutation
defined in [§5/§7.3 of the spec](#architecture) (odd stride over a
power-of-two shard count ⇒ 64 DISTINCT shards; lane 0 is the directory's own
inode shard):

64 independent Raft leaders is the same throughput budget deemed sufficient
for the hottest single file, and it makes the used-shard set a **64-bit
bitmap on the directory's inode row** — a bounded `stat()` collect, by
construction rather than by hope. Global spread is unchanged: different
directories get different strides and different home shards, so a million
directories still cover all 4096 shards.

**First use of a dir lane touches the parent shard — the one exception.**
"The parent shard is not involved" holds for steady state, not for the first
mutation to land on a given lane: that one registers the lane in the
directory's used-shard bitmap, carried inside the transaction it is already
part of, exactly like `active_lanes` activation for files. It happens at
most 64 times in a directory's lifetime, so it is not a rate-proportional
cost. Without it `stat(dir)` could miss a shard that holds a newer mtime.

**Directory `utimens` needs the same generation fence as a file's.** An
explicit backwards mtime on a directory cannot stick while older
`dir_lane.max_mtime` values are still visible to the reduction, so the
directory inode row carries `dir_mtime_gen`, only `utimens` bumps it, and
the bump is distributed to the used lanes by the same bounded fence
(≤65 authorities) — the directory analogue of the inode fence in
[data.md](#appendix-10--protocol--data-plane). As with files, ctime needs no generation.

The reduction is validated by the same double-collect protocol as
file `stat()`, and the reductions are transaction payload rather than
exclusive keys ([transactions.md](#appendix-9--protocol--cross-shard-transactions)) — two creates on
different hash shards must not conflict merely because both touch the
directory's time.

Explicit changes (`utimens`, `chmod`, `chown` on the directory itself) go to
the inode row's `base_*` values under `mtime_gen`, exactly as for files.

### RMDIR and RENAME are not uniformly cheap once a directory is HASHED

The operation→participant matrix in the spec gives the common case; the
spread layout changes two entries, and the difference is worth stating
explicitly because both are easy to get wrong.

**RMDIR must prove emptiness, and on a HASHED directory emptiness is
distributed.** For a LOCAL directory, "no entries" is a single range check on
one shard, so RMDIR is the ordinary two-shard transaction (parent dentry +
directory inode row). For a HASHED directory the entries are spread over the
directory's hash shards, and a naive per-shard check races: shard A can be
observed empty, then get a create, while shard B is being checked. So:

```text
RMDIR on LOCAL dir:   2 shards (parent dentry + inode row)
RMDIR on HASHED dir:  parent dentry + inode row
                      + a transactional read over the directory's dentry
                        shards, whose emptiness is part of the transaction's
                        read set (conditional PREPARE; any concurrent create
                        invalidates it and the RMDIR retries or fails
                        ENOTEMPTY)
```

The alternative — maintaining an exact distributed entry count — would
re-create a per-directory counter hotspot on the very directory that was
spread to avoid one. RMDIR is rare; paying an O(hash-shard-count)
transaction for it is the right trade, and the operation is bounded because
the used-shard set is recorded on the directory inode.

**Same-directory RENAME is not always single-shard.** In a LOCAL directory,
old and new name share the parent's shard, so a simple rename is one entry.
In a HASHED directory `hash(parent, old)` and `hash(parent, new)` are
independent, so the ordinary case is a **two-shard transaction**, widening
further if the destination exists and its inode row lives elsewhere.

### Directory rename must not create a cycle

POSIX forbids moving a directory beneath itself: the source may not be an
ancestor of the destination. Checking this by walking the tree at the moment
of the rename is **not sufficient under concurrency** — two concurrent
renames can each validate against a tree that was legal when they read it,
and together produce a detached cycle that no single operation ever
authorized:

```text
initially:   /a  and  /b  are siblings
rename(/a -> /b/a)   validates: b is not under a     OK
rename(/b -> /a/b)   validates: a is not under b     OK
both commit  ->  a and b are now each other's ancestor, unreachable
```

The fix is to make the **entire ancestry predicate part of the transaction's
read set**, so the two renames above are forced to conflict. Every directory
inode row carries an authoritative `parent_dir` pointer with a
`parent_version` that changes on every reparent:

```text
directory rename(src, dst):
  1. walk dst's ancestors to the root, collecting
     (dir_id, parent_version) for every link in the chain
  2. fail EINVAL if src appears anywhere in that chain
  3. include the whole collected chain in the conditional PREPARE as
     read-set entries at those versions
  4. any concurrent rename that reparents a directory in the chain bumps
     its parent_version -> our prepare fails its version check
  5. abort and retry
```

That makes the check a real concurrency-controlled predicate rather than an
advisory glance. The cost is an O(depth) multi-shard transaction — acceptable
precisely because directory rename is rare, and unavoidable if the invariant
"the namespace is a tree" (I8's structural half) is to hold under concurrent
renames. Renaming a *file* is unaffected: files have no children, so no
ancestry predicate exists.


## Appendix 12 — Protocol — sessions, open-unlinked, locking

*Source: `how-it-works/protocols/sessions.md` (headers demoted, nav stripped, links rebased to `docs/how-it-works/`).* **Authority: normative protocol.**

**Implementation scope:** this page specifies the accepted design, not a
current deployment guarantee. The [public-path review](../status/spec-implementation.md)
records persistence, session, fixed-profile/repair and integrity limitations;
consult those gates before claiming this contract is implemented. Session and
revocation reads also depend on fresh quorum authority
([W82](#w82)), not a cached completed read index.

[Architecture](#architecture) · [Transactions](#appendix-9--protocol--cross-shard-transactions) ·
[Data protocol](#appendix-10--protocol--data-plane)

These four mechanisms share one foundation: a real client-session protocol.
It is specified here together with everything built on it.

### Client sessions and fencing

Several mechanisms — distributed locks, open-unlinked inode lifetime, append
reservation recovery, duplicate suppression — all depend on one magic
transition: "the client incarnation becomes stale." That transition is a
real protocol, because the naive version is one of the hardest problems in
distributed filesystems: **a network partition is indistinguishable from a
dead client**, and reclaiming a merely-partitioned client's locks or open
files on a timeout alone would change authoritative state on the word of a
failure detector.

**The protocol.** Every client operates under a **session**:

```text
session = { client_uuid, session_epoch, state }     (committed via Raft)
session authority for a client = shard hash(client_uuid) & 0xFFF
```

- Session records live on **sharded session authorities** (not one global
  session server — that would be a serializer and a single point of
  failure). A mount establishes its session with a Raft-committed epoch.
- Every mutating request carries `(client_uuid, session_epoch, op_id)`.
  **Shard leaders fence on the epoch**: a request naming a session epoch
  older than the committed one is rejected as stale (P3 — stale work is
  harmless, never accepted as authoritative). A leader answers from locally
  established session authority (below) — never from a cache it merely hopes
  is fresh, and never from a clock.
  **Data targets do not fence sessions.** A fenced client can still PUT an
  immutable candidate fragment — harmlessly: the target stores an orphan,
  and the metadata authority rejects its publication, so it never becomes
  visible (exactly P3, and exactly the "targets are dumb" model of
  [the data protocol](#appendix-10--protocol--data-plane)). Synchronously validating session authority
  on every data target would put an RPC/cache-coherence problem on the
  fastest path for zero correctness benefit.
- **The failure detector and the authority are separate roles:** heartbeat
  loss / connection death only decides *when* a session replacement may be
  **attempted**; **consensus decides *which* session is authoritative** —
  the epoch bump is a Raft commit on the session shard. A timeout alone
  never changes anything.
- Once the epoch bump has passed the **revocation barrier** below, the old
  session is dead everywhere: its **POSIX locks** are reclaimed by the lock
  authorities, its **open-unlinked leases** are dropped (the orphan inode
  becomes reclaimable, below), its pending **append reservations** are
  resolved as committed zero holes ([data protocol](#appendix-10--protocol--data-plane)), and its
  **dedup records are retained** so its in-flight retries are still
  recognized as duplicates rather than re-executed (I16).
- A fenced client learns on its next operation (`FENCED`) and must
  re-establish a session (new epoch, re-open state) before doing further
  work.

**The honest trade-off:** a partitioned-but-alive client can be fenced —
that is an availability sacrifice, never a safety violation, and it is the
standard fencing-token pattern (the session epoch *is* the fencing token,
checked at every authority). The alternative — never fencing on suspicion —
leaves dead clients' locks and reservations held forever.

#### Revocation is a barrier, not an announcement

Committing `epoch+1` on the session shard does **not**, by itself, fence
anything. Metadata shards are independent Raft groups; a shard that has not
heard about `epoch+1` and is willing to act on its own cached view of epoch
`E` can still commit a mutation for the old client *after* the bump —
directly violating I23. "Leaders re-validate on doubt" is not a protocol,
because nothing tells a leader it should be in doubt.

So session state is a three-phase transition with a real barrier, and the
session record carries the set of shards that could possibly act on it:

```text
ACTIVE(E)  ->  FENCING(E+1)  ->  ACTIVE(E+1)

session record:
    { client_uuid, session_epoch, state, touched_shards }

touched_shards: a 4096-bit bitmap — bounded, and small (512 B)
```

**Registration (first use of a session on a shard).** Before shard S accepts
epoch E as authoritative, S must be recorded in that session's
`touched_shards`:

```text
S receives a mutation naming (client_uuid, E), and has no local record:
    S asks the session authority to register S for (client_uuid, E)
    session authority Raft-commits the bitmap bit
    -> only then may S cache "E is authoritative" and proceed
```

If the session authority and S share one Raft group, one committed command
may atomically record the bitmap bit and S's established epoch. Apply must
recheck the current ACTIVE epoch, preserve the rejection floor and respect
prepared key ownership. A preceding FENCING entry rejects this admission; a
following FENCING entry sees the committed participant. Different Raft groups
retain registration before establishment; missing rows never imply authority.

This is **once per (session, shard)**, not per request: a client that works
against 200 shards pays 200 registrations over the life of its mount. The
hot path is unaffected — an established shard answers from its own committed
state with no session lookup at all.

**Fencing.**

```text
1. session authority Raft-commits FENCING(E+1)
      -> no new shard may register for E from this point
2. touched_shards(E) is frozen by that same commit
3. FENCE(E+1) is sent to every shard in the frozen set
4. each shard, durably:
      rejects epoch E from now on
      resolves or aborts that session's undecided work
      ACKs the fence
5. only after every shard in the set has ACKed:
      session authority Raft-commits ACTIVE(E+1)
6. locks, open leases and append reservations of E may now be reclaimed,
   and the new session may begin authoritative work
```

Step 5 is the barrier: **nothing that depends on the old session being dead
may happen before it.** If a touched shard cannot be reached or cannot
establish authority, the new session **waits** — the correct
availability-for-safety trade, and not a new availability loss in practice,
since a shard that cannot establish authority cannot commit for the old
client either.

Note what this protocol deliberately avoids: it puts **no session lookup on
the I/O path**. Registration is once per shard per session; the barrier runs
only during recovery. Normal operations proceed on locally established
authority, which is exactly why the fence has to be explicit — nobody is
checking anything per request.

#### Mutation coverage (K5: W134 with W72)

Every metadata mutation a mount sends names its session, and every apply
that changes session-owned state checks it. There is no stand-in identity,
no "absent row means OK" path and no compatibility switch.

**Mount lifecycle.**

```text
mount:        random client_uuid, epoch 1; CREATE the session on its owner
              shard (Raft commit). Mount fails if the cluster refuses it.
first use     the client (HOLD, FLOCK, APPEND, publication, REPORT, PUT
of a shard:   ticket, SETATTR, XATTR) or the serving host (namespace ops)
              REGISTERs the shard in touched_shards on the owner, then
              ESTABLISHes it on the shard (one REGISTER_ESTABLISH entry when
              both share a Raft group). The client caches the shard bit.
UNREGISTERED: the shard has no established row for this epoch. The client
              forgets the cached bit, admits the shard again and resends
              the same identity once.
FENCED:       the shard's rejection floor (or a newer established epoch)
              is above the request epoch. The mount stops mutating: every
              later mutation fails EIO locally without an RPC, and no
              request is ever resent under the old epoch.
unknown:      the owner has no session for this uuid (never created, or
              the cluster was re-formatted). Hosts never create a session
              on a client's behalf; the refusal is UNREGISTERED at the
              owner and the client treats it as FENCED.
```

The operation-ID retry identity (I16) is unchanged: a retry keeps its
`(uuid, epoch, seq)`, and the session check runs before any recorded
verdict is returned, so a fenced identity cannot read back a retained
result.

**Refusal codes.** `efs_session_accept` is the single local check.

| Local state on the shard | Result | Inode RPC status | FUSE errno |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| no row for the uuid | `EFS_ERR_UNREGISTERED` | `UNREGISTERED` (15) | re-admit once, else `EIO` |
| established epoch below the request | `EFS_ERR_UNREGISTERED` | `UNREGISTERED` (15) | re-admit once, else `EIO` |
| request epoch below the rejection floor | `EFS_ERR_FENCED` | `FENCED` (14) | `EIO`, mount fenced |
| established epoch above the request | `EFS_ERR_FENCED` | `FENCED` (14) | `EIO`, mount fenced |
| established epoch equals the request | `EFS_OK` | — | — |

**Coverage.** "Wire" is what the request carries. "Admit" is who registers
the touched shard. "Apply" names the replicated check that refuses the
identity after a fence, so a check that passed before proposal cannot
let a fenced mutation commit.

| Path | Wire | Admit | Apply check | Before K5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CREATE, MKDIR | opid suffix (mandatory) | host, served dentry shard | `efs_session_prepare_namespace` / opid window | opid optional; host created unknown sessions |
| retained CREATE (FUSE) | `efs_opid_req` in the request | host | same | already mandatory |
| UNLINK, RMDIR | opid suffix (mandatory) | host | same | opid optional |
| LINK | opid suffix (mandatory) | host | same | opid optional |
| RENAME_AT | opid suffix (mandatory) | host | same | opid optional |
| SETATTR size (truncate, D25) | opid suffix (mandatory) | client, inode shard | opid window on the inode shard | apply used the legacy accept |
| SETATTR mode/uid/gid | opid suffix (mandatory) | client, inode shard | SETATTR command session bytes | no identity |
| SETATTR times (utimens) | opid suffix (mandatory) | client, inode shard | UTIMENS command session bytes (inode copy) | no identity |
| XATTR set/remove | session suffix (mandatory) | client, inode shard | XATTR command session bytes | no identity |
| HOLD open/close (lease) | session suffix (mandatory) | client, inode shard | `efs_lease_open` | suffix optional, stand-in UUID |
| CREATE with `EFS_CREATE_F_HOLD` | opid suffix (mandatory) | host | lease key bound to the request session | stand-in UUID from owner |
| FLOCK / fcntl grant | session suffix (mandatory) | client, inode shard | `efs_lock_grant` | suffix optional, stand-in UUID |
| FLOCK / fcntl release, GETLK | session suffix (mandatory) | — | host gate before release; GETLK is a read | suffix optional |
| APPEND reservation | opid + ACK suffix (mandatory) | client, inode shard | `efs_meta_capture_append` / append apply | absent suffix accepted |
| lease edges (OPEN/CLOSE/CLEAR_PENDING, D25) | identity in command | client | guarded edge apply | already strict |
| publication / admit / retire (D25) | identity in request | client | publication apply | already strict |
| PUT ticket admit / retire | identity in ticket | client | ticket apply | already strict |
| REPORT_CHUNKS | session suffix (mandatory) | client, lane shards | REPORT mapping/activation guards | suffix optional |
| lane bootstrap | none | — | none | none |
| data PUT / DATA_COMMIT | none | — | none (targets do not fence) | none |
| `efs-mgmt` raft-* smoke commands | own session, created per call | mgmt | same as the path it drives | none |

Lane bootstrap only creates the empty lane rows a file's layout already
implies; it changes no user-visible state, so it is not session-scoped.
Data targets do not fence by design; the metadata publication that would
make a fenced write visible is refused instead. The raw command submit
RPC (`efs-mgmt raft-submit`, session commands) proposes commands whose
apply checks are listed above; it is an operator interface, not a client
path, and a command without session bytes is refused by those applies.

**Transaction-owned paths.** Multi-shard transactions (regular-file
utimens, APPEND reservation and completion, session-owned barrier
retirement) prepare the inode shard's local session row with its unchanged
exact image ahead of the plan. The executor authorizes that image from its
own bytes (`session_owner_capture` in `src/meta/append_plan.c`, the
`efs_session_accept` rules) before preparing it. A check on one read and a
CAS on a later read would let a fence landing between them become the
comparison base. A fence after the capture fails the owner PREPARE; a
fence after the PREPARE waits behind the intent until the transaction
resolves.

**Client latch.** The mount's `session_started` and `session_fenced` flags
are read without a lock on every mutation, so every access is atomic
(acquire loads, release store, and an exchange that elects the one fencer
that logs).

#### Duplicate suppression must be bounded state

I16 requires that a replayed mutation cannot apply twice, and the fencing
rules above require dedup records to survive an epoch bump. At billions of
files and trillions of RPCs that must **not** mean one permanent row per
operation — that is an unbounded, permanently growing table on every shard.
The retained state is a window, not a history:

```text
per (client_uuid, session_epoch) on each shard that served it:
    highest_contiguous_seq      one integer: everything at or below is done
    completion window           small bitmap for out-of-order completions
                                above the watermark
    bounded reply cache         responses for the few in-flight ops that
                                could still be retried
```

A request at or below `highest_contiguous_seq` is a duplicate by definition
and needs no per-op record. Only the ragged edge — operations completed out
of order above the watermark — costs a bit each, and the window is bounded
by the client's allowed in-flight depth.

**Reclamation is driven by acknowledgement, not by elapsed time.** The
failure model allows a message to be delayed arbitrarily and duplicated
([the spec §2](#architecture)), so no timer can *prove* that a
straggler will not arrive — a "retention window" would be an assumption the
network never agreed to. The client instead carries a **response-ack
watermark**: the **highest *contiguous*** sequence number whose reply it has
received, and the shard may release result state at or below it. Contiguity
is not pedantry — replies arrive out of order, so a watermark defined as
"the highest sequence whose reply arrived" would let reply 100 arriving
before 99 authorize discarding 99's result while 99's retry is still in
flight. A later duplicate at or below the watermark is then answered as
already-completed — cheaply, and without re-executing.

The reply cache matters more than it first appears, because for some
operations "it already happened" is not a sufficient answer. If an
`O_APPEND` reservation reply is lost, the retry of that same op-ID must
recover **the same offset** — a fresh reservation would allocate a second
range and leave a permanent hole. The retained reply, not merely a
completion bit, is what makes the retry idempotent.

For a **live** session, records are reclaimable once the client's ack
watermark has passed them. For a **fenced** one, requiring the watermark too
would leak forever: a dead client never sends another acknowledgement, so
its reply state could never be released. The revocation barrier is what
makes that unnecessary — once `epoch+1` is committed and every touched shard
has been fenced, a request carrying the **old epoch** is rejected on the
epoch alone, without consulting any per-request state. So the rule is:

```text
live session      release at or below the ack watermark
fenced session    once the revocation barrier has completed and the
                  outstanding ambiguity is resolved, drop the whole
                  epoch's dedup state — old-epoch requests are rejected
                  by epoch, not by lookup
```

Transaction decision records
([transactions.md](#appendix-9--protocol--cross-shard-transactions)) have the matching condition:
reclaimable once every participant has acknowledged the decision and no
recovering participant can still ask for it.

#### Ambiguous completion is resolved by identity (W155)

A request whose reply was lost after it was sent, or whose retry budget ran
out after a send, has an **unknown** outcome: the server may have applied
it. The client never turns that into an error by guessing. Before failing
it resolves the request against its receipt, under the **same identity**
and a fresh bounded window (`EFS_RESOLVE_MS`, default 8 s):

```text
identified directory op    receipt = the op-id window above (durable)
  (CREATE/UNLINK/LINK/      re-send the identical request: a completed id is
   RENAME_AT)               answered from the window, a new one runs once
REPORT_CHUNKS (sync)       receipt = per-host table keyed by (session,
                            publication id), in memory and bounded
                            ask each host the REPORT reached
                            (EFS_REPORT_F_RECEIPT, runs nothing):
                              applied  -> success
                              partial  -> STALE (replay the CAS losers)
                              pending  -> wait and ask again
                              else     -> re-send the same publication id
```

The REPORT receipt is not in Raft on purpose (an entry per REPORT would undo
K32). Its absence (eviction, a restarted or different host) is never read
as "not applied": the same publication id is sent again, which the REPORT
path already makes idempotent (a committed record skips, a W77 unit joins
its deterministic transaction). A duplicate that reaches a host while the
first attempt still runs there joins it instead of running beside it.

Only an outcome still unknown when the window ends is an error (EIO for a
flush or close), and the client line says so with the request identity
(`report-resolve id=… outcome=unknown`, `inode-rpc: resolve … outcome=unknown`).
The server lines carry the same identity (`report-receipt`, `opid-receipt`),
so a failure, its retries and the server's verdict join exactly. Nothing
here assumes rollback or old-or-new atomicity: a resolved request is the
server's recorded verdict, an unresolved one stays unknown.

### Open-unlinked inode lifetime

I6/I7 allow `nlink = 0` while a file is open. The lifecycle:

```text
nlink -> 0            => inode enters ORPHAN state
valid open references => still readable/writable (I19)
reclaim only when     nlink == 0 AND no valid open reference can exist
```

**All of this state is keyed by `FileID = (ino, inode_generation)`, not by
`ino`.** The data plane already scopes every object by the file's
incarnation ([data.md](#appendix-10--protocol--data-plane)); inode-scoped *ephemeral* state needs the
same protection, and for the same reason. An ino is reclaimed and reissued;
a delayed CLOSE, UNLOCK, or reservation-resolution naming `(ino=100, gen=7)`
must not touch `(ino=100, gen=8)`, or one file's straggler silently releases
another file's lock or drops its open reference. The rule is general: **an
operation acting through an inode handle validates the inode generation
before it changes anything**, and a generation mismatch is a stale-handle
error, never a successful no-op.

Open/close must **not** become heavyweight durable metadata mutations on the
hot path. The mechanism is **one session-scoped open lease per
(FileID, session)** — not one mutation per file descriptor:

```text
session's FIRST open of an inode:
    inode authority (inode_shard) Raft-commits  add open_session(session_id)
further local opens/dups of the same inode:
    free — tracked inside the client session, no metadata mutation
session's LAST close of the inode:
    inode authority commits  remove open_session(session_id)
session fenced:
    its open_session entries are stale; any authority may lazily verify
    against the session authority and drop them

reclaim when:  nlink == 0  AND  open_sessions == empty
```

This deliberately puts open-lifetime coordination on the inode shard, but
only **once per session/file lifetime** — not per I/O and not per
descriptor. That is a semantic serialization (P1): the coordination exists
because POSIX open-unlinked semantics require it, and it costs one Raft
entry at each end of a session's use of a file. A fenced (dead) client's
leases are safely retired by recovery, and a stale session's lease can
neither keep an inode alive nor be reused (I19). Reclaim is L6.

The production FUSE CREATE path combines its first OPEN with clearing the
exact pending-CREATE token in one sequenced lease edge. It retains the
exact combined edge and pending token while that edge is unresolved. A proven successful
edge settles adoption before releasing that ownership; cleanup first proves the
same edge, then compensates its OPEN with CLOSE and avoids a duplicate
CLEAR_PENDING. A proven negative OPEN leaves ordinary pending-token cleanup
responsible for the CREATE. Existing local open ownership retains the
separate adoption path, and all waits share the caller’s original deadline.

### Distributed POSIX locking

`fcntl()` byte-range locks and `flock()` must have **one global lock state**
across clients — a lock taken on client A must conflict with a lock requested
on client B. POSIX advisory locks do not fence ordinary reads/writes (an
application that ignores locks is allowed to), so the data path is untouched;
but every participating lock request must see the same authoritative state.

- **One lock authority per inode.** Lock state for a file lives on
  `inode_shard(ino)`, as `(FileID, start, end, owner)` records with overlap
  conflict checking, mutated through that shard's Raft log. This deliberately
  serializes lock *management* for one file — acceptable, because an
  application using record locks has explicitly asked for coordination; it is
  a semantic serialization (P1), not an accidental one. Splitting arbitrary
  overlapping ranges across shards is rejected: range overlap is not
  partitionable, and the common case (whole-file `flock`, small-range
  `fcntl`) is cheap on one authority.
- **Owner identity is per namespace, because Linux ownership is.** A single
  process-based owner token would model only classic `fcntl()`. Both
  `flock()` locks and OFD `fcntl()` locks are associated with the **open
  file description**, so duplicated descriptors (and descriptors inherited
  across `fork`) *share* them, while classic `fcntl()` locks are owned by
  the process and are dropped by closing any descriptor for the file. The
  owner token therefore differs by namespace:

  ```text
  classic fcntl  -> (client_uuid, session_epoch, process_id)
  OFD fcntl      -> (client_uuid, session_epoch, open_description_id)
  flock          -> (client_uuid, session_epoch, open_description_id)
  ```

  The client assigns a stable `open_description_id` per open file
  description and reuses it across `dup`/`fork`, which is what makes shared
  ownership work across a cluster. Locks are released on close/process exit
  as usual; a *dead client* is handled by the session protocol above — once
  its session is fenced, the lock authority reclaims every lock owned under
  that epoch, whichever namespace. Blocked waiters are woken in order.
- **Lock conflict domains (Linux target, stated precisely).** There are
  **two conflict domains, not three namespaces** — a distinction that is
  easy to get wrong, because the three lock *kinds* do not map one-to-one
  onto them:

  ```text
  record-lock domain (one domain, two ownership kinds)
      classic fcntl   owner = (client_uuid, session_epoch, process_id)
      OFD fcntl       owner = (client_uuid, session_epoch, open_description_id)
      -> the two kinds CONFLICT with each other by byte range, even
         within one process on one file descriptor

  flock domain
      flock           owner = (client_uuid, session_epoch, open_description_id)
      -> independent of the record-lock domain
  ```

  Ownership and conflict are separate questions. Classic and OFD `fcntl`
  locks differ in *who owns them* and in when they are released (any close
  vs. last close of the description), but they are the same kind of record
  lock and a conflicting pair blocks — POSIX.1-2024 specifies this for OFD
  locks, and Linux has behaved this way since 3.15. So the authority
  evaluates both kinds against one another in a single byte-range domain,
  keyed only by owner token. `flock()` is the genuinely separate one: it is
  not POSIX, and its independence from record locks is **Linux behavior**
  that efs reproduces because it targets Linux. Locks owned by an
  open file description are shared by duplicated and inherited descriptors
  in both domains. When a session is fenced, every lock owned under that
  epoch is reclaimed, in both domains.

#### Blocking waits: the wait lives on the authority

`F_SETLKW` and blocking `flock` are where "distributed" stops being a
placement detail. The protocol:

```text
client -> lock authority (the inode's shard leader):
          LOCKW(FileID, range, type, owner, op_id)
    conflicting -> the request stays OPEN at the leader; the waiter enters
                   an in-memory queue in arrival order
    grantable   -> the lock record commits via Raft; the held RPC replies
release/unlock -> the leader scans the queue in FIFO order and grants every
                  waiter whose request no longer conflicts; a waiter that
                  still conflicts stays queued
```

- **The grant is the reply.** A blocking lock request is a long-lived RPC
  the leader answers only when the lock is granted or the wait fails. No
  polling, no client-side retry loop, no timer. The wait queue is leader
  memory, not Raft state: a wait has no durability value (the client can
  always re-ask), and replicating it would put lock *contention* on the
  WAL.
- **Fairness rule.** Grants are made in arrival order; a still-conflicting
  waiter does not block non-conflicting requests behind it — except that a
  queued *exclusive* request stops later overlapping *shared* requests from
  being granted ahead of it, so an exclusive waiter cannot be starved by a
  shared-lock stream. POSIX requires no fairness at all; this is the
  cheapest rule that makes starvation impossible rather than merely
  unlikely.
- **Failover: the client re-issues, and the op-id makes it safe.** If the
  lock authority's leader changes while a wait is outstanding, the held
  request fails with it; the client re-issues the *same* `(op_id)` request
  to the new leader. Idempotency (I16) covers the case where the old leader
  committed the grant just before failing — the re-issued request finds the
  recorded grant and returns it instead of queueing again. FIFO order is
  not preserved across a failover; failover is rare, and fairness is
  policy, not correctness.
- **A fenced waiter is dequeued and never granted.** The revocation barrier
  already requires every touched shard to "resolve or abort that session's
  undecided work"; a queued lock wait is exactly that. The fence drops the
  queue entry and fails the held RPC, so a dead client's blocked syscall
  cannot wedge behind a lock it will never release, and a session fenced
  while waiting is never granted the lock.
- **Interruption cancels by op-id.** A signal (`EINTR`) aborts the wait
  locally; the client sends a cancel naming the wait's op-id. The cancel is
  idempotent: if the grant raced the cancel, the client owns the lock and
  simply unlocks it.

#### Range algebra is POSIX's, unchanged, on one authority

Because every record for one inode lives on one shard, the authority runs
exactly the local algorithm:

- a record covers `[start, end]`; `flock` is the whole-file range in its
  own domain;
- a partial unlock **splits** a record; adjacent same-owner, same-type
  records **merge**;
- a type change (`F_RDLCK`→`F_WRLCK`, `LOCK_SH`→`LOCK_EX`) converts in
  place, or queues like any other request while a conflict remains;
- `F_GETLK` is a leader read (no Raft entry) reporting the first
  conflicting record — the owner mapped back to a client-local pid for
  classic `fcntl` — or `F_UNLCK`.

**Resource bound.** Splitting makes the per-inode record count adversarial
— a process can lock and unlock alternating bytes and grow the table
without bound. The authority caps records per inode and returns `ENOLCK`
past the cap; that is the POSIX error for exactly this condition.

#### Deadlock detection: same-inode only — and that is conformant

POSIX lists `EDEADLK` under errors `F_SETLKW` **may** fail with, not shall,
and Linux itself detects deadlock cycles only for classic `fcntl` locks
(OFD `fcntl` and `flock` waits are never checked). efs matches that
exactly:

- **Same-inode cycles are detected.** The lock authority holds the complete
  wait-for graph for its inode — the holder set plus its wait queue — so a
  cycle among byte ranges of one file is caught and the incoming request
  fails `EDEADLK`.
- **Cross-inode cycles are not detected.** A cycle spanning two files can
  span two shards and two clients, and no single authority ever sees the
  whole cycle; a distributed wait-for protocol is rejected as cost and
  complexity on a path that is rare and self-inflicted. This is conformant
  because detection is a MAY — and no wait is ever *stuck*: every blocked
  wait is interruptible by signal and is torn down by session fencing, so a
  deadlocked application can always be killed out of it.


## Appendix 13 — Performance — multi-Raft runtime & hot-path contract

*Source: `how-it-works/performance.md` (headers demoted, nav stripped, links rebased to `docs/how-it-works/`).* **Authority: normative protocol.**

**Scope:** the execution rules below are design requirements, not a claim
that the current two-group/worker runtime implements every rule. See
[W66 and public-path limits](../status/spec-implementation.md). Dated fcstor
measurements do not identify the running NUC/xorinox topology or establish
W71 durability; local engine studies are separate from FUSE/cluster results.

The topology in [the spec](#architecture) makes linear scaling
*possible*. This document is the contract that makes it *actual* — the
difference between "the architecture scales" and "the implementation
scales." Each item is a requirement, traceable to P1/P4, not a tuning
suggestion.

### The multi-Raft runtime

**4096 logical groups are not 4096 physical mini-databases.** A node must
never run per-group timers, WALs, fsyncs, sockets, heartbeats, or threads —
on a 3-node cluster that would be ~1365 leaders per node doing bookkeeping
instead of work. The implementation is a **multi-Raft runtime**: a few
reactor threads (per NUMA domain, P4) drive many shard state machines; Raft
messages are batched by destination, heartbeats coalesced, AppendEntries
pipelined, WAL writes group-committed across groups, and KV applies batched —
while each shard keeps its own independent logical ordering, terms, and
commit indices. This is the same logical/physical split as the applied-state
KV (§5 of the spec), and it is an architectural requirement, not an
